The asymmetry is painful… even [Jonathan Haidt’s moral foundations framework](https://www.facebook.com/jonathanhaidt/photos/my-colleagues-and-i-revised-moral-foundations-theory-to-do-a-better-job-of-expla/2079950535564617/) [results](https://yukaichou.com/behavioral-analysis/moral-foundations-theory-haidt-care-fairness-loyalty/) are pretty clear on this: conservatives can “speak” more moral languages than progressives can, progressives who are, quite *literally*, less empathetic in the strict meaning of the word. 

Fuck the boomers. Fuck the left. And fuck the academics.

***

## OK, back to business: Can You Own a Forest?

Jonathon Moses and Anne Margrethe Brigham started this [(same!) chapter](https://stacker.news/items/1565551) with a cool, provocative, absurd question about owning the sun. Of course **nobody does (or can) own the sun**, or block anybody else from accessing sunlight (When I mentioned this to Ben in Helsinki, he snarled something like "just wait for it!" or "with enough tech, they will!" again betraying a complete understanding of capital conditions and economic scarcity... **it's not tech or law**, it's E-C-O-N-O-M-I-C-S.)

...

![](https://m.stacker.news/160211)

Of course you can *own a forest*, in precisely the same way you can own a chainsaw.

I have greater **possession** over the chainsaw, seeing as how it's in my basement (which I may or may not, according to these authors' twisted logic, own), and it's smaller in size, so I can physically move it, *possess it* in a way I can't a forest (=doesn't fit in my hand, doesn't have a handle). The forest, however, is out *there* and -- if the stackers will allow the pun -- *rooted in place*. But what do any of those things have to do with ownership?

Ownership (=property) is a social relationship about who gets to do what. More to the point, it's the amount of violence someone exerts on you if you break that ownership bond... steal my chainsaw, let's say; burn down my forest. 

The authors cite Honoré (1961) from an Oxford jurisprudence essay on the 11(!) *incidents* of property but it all comes down to the one single, social-cooperation and social-harmony (shout-out HHH) aspect: **who decides what a good, asset, or thing does when there are rival, mutually exclusive claims/wishes on it?** 
Your car isn't used for the majority of the day/week... what's the reason, economically or philosophically, that [someone else can't "borrow](https://mises.org/free-market/case-hoarding)" it in the meantime? Some worthy cause like a homeless guy napping in there to avoid the rain, let's say. 

Economically speaking, ownership is optionality. Basically: rivalrousness and excludability rule everything. (Which, if you've ever delved down the economic rabbit hole of the social calculation debate as I have, is *the* [components on which everything turn](https://www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning).)

## Ownership is, like the authors partially outline in this section, the right or first-lien decision on how the item/good/resource is and can be used.

> What we think of as 'private property' in nature is really an abstract bundle of rights that governments grant to individuals or communities. (pp. 36-37)

Ah yes, just how the government owns your house and a government can rescind/take/expropriate any of your stuff at any point.

The fact that they are restricted from doing this by a legal system concerned with whose property is used by whom is SORT OF the definition of a legal order: *rule of law, individual liberty* etc etc. If none of those words have meaning, and the *default* mode of ownership is 100% ruled by the government (who, I'm convinced the authors say while suppressing a laughter, *represent you, the people*), there is no legal order: only (military) might makes right. If so: ***what in the world are we doing here?!***

Look, the fact that a government can rescind or override property claims — practically, physically, militarily, or even "legally" — doesn't invalidate that ownership or property exists (dare I say *precede?!*) irrespective of a government. It doesn't therefore follow that *no* property claims are real; that all ownership is provisional or resort/revert to a government if and when it so chooses.

Or, if you wanna go to that insanity: **Bitcoin.**

By this insane theory (that government owns everything, and it just *lets* you pretend that what is yours is temporarily yours), *nothing* is owned by anybody ever. Oh, but that UTXO somehow refuses to move; you can "own" it all you want, hashtag [New York Finder's Keepers example](https://stacker.news/items/1498602), but it changes nothing about the world. If I hold the private key to a UTXO that you "own" I can move it nonetheless; tell you to royally fuck off in the OP\_RETURN.

As always, Bitcoin stands unique here. Being a commodity without physical dimensions — [element zero, in Knut Svanholm’s phrasing](https://mises.org/mises-wire/sebag-and-natural-money) — it is the first and only thing you can truly own. Not own in a *legal* sense, because Bitcoin, the blockchain, doesn’t care what your laws say: You may have *legal title* to some UTXO, but it matters not.

In fact, and Stephen Kinsella said this directly and uncompromisingly [on stage in Helsinki, too](https://stacker.news/items/1585380): Bitcoin, being *pure information*, cannot be owned. It’s technically and praxeologically speaking just secret information, available and open to all, just accessible to almost nobody.

All you have when you have a UTXO is a highly probabilistic *asymmetric* ability to move funds. Baseline, everyone has some (exceedingly low) probability to spend a given UTXO. You, holding the private key or the seed phrase backup, have a much larger probability — prob-***ability*** — to spend. The entire legalistic edifice of rights goes out the window: it’s *all* ability; possession becoming [ten-tenths of the law.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possession_is_nine-tenths_of_the_law)

For analogy, my chess brain went to Magnus Carlsen. He has no “right” to win every chess game against chess low-lifes like me; if we were pitted against each other for a trophy, the victory isn’t his *by right*. It’s his by ability: through his superior (asymmetric) information and skill, he will win every time. Just like *your* UTXO is secured by *your* superior ability to move it relative to mine.

***

And when the moronic morons couldn't get worse... *they found a lower low*:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160212)

## Why would (3) be the "default setting," you absolute twatheads?

Or in meme form: **when did** [**this become the default**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ch5_j2q8ZPI)**?!**

If all you wanted to do and say with this book was, *All Your Stuff Are Belong To Us*, then why the hell dress it up like this? How in the world could anybody, for more than a fleeting moment, consider that the *default* ownership position of everything is *the government*?! Plain-old theft and power grabs, masquerading as political philosophy and under the cover of academic intellectualizing.

Fuck.
Right.
Off.

***

Serious retort: I might as well say that (4) — or (1) — is the default setting, and that every government action to restrict, regulate, tax, or otherwise impose on this immaculate conception is in violation of rights and reason.

And stop with this passive-tense hidden-actor nonsense ("...is assigned"): no sex is "assigned" at birth; no income is "distributed" (h/t Rothbard) separately from production; and property rights to goods that are yours are not "assigned" by some prior tribunal, deciding the starting blocks for everyone else.

> As nature belongs to us in common, our representatives in government authorize this private 'taking'. They do this to keep the peace and protect the resources (from either inefficient or over-exploitation), for the benefit of the community they represent. (p. 37)

oh lord. *Please grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change (=other people's moronic ideas and their pathetically limited intellectual stature), and the strength to resist committing the vile damage I wish to inflict upon these fuckheads, ... and perhaps the wisdom to know to which books to direct my attention.*

*TL;DR*: **left-wing people are not impressive; academics are full of it/themselves; this book is the trashiest nonsense bullshit intellectual nonsense I've ever had the misfortune to stumble across (...with the possible exception of the *Capitalism* book.** https://stacker.news/items/1561710**,** https://stacker.news/items/1562148**)**

items.title: Using Bitcoin Miners to Make Maple Syrup
items.text:
Immersion mining with canola oil to concentrate maple sap more quickly
![](https://v.nostr.build/n997.mp4)
I'm using a single S9 hash board immersed in canola oil to heat maple sap to increase the effectiveness of the reverse osmosis sap concentration system.
![](https://i.nostr.build/okkw.jpg)
The weather conditions this season have caused the maple sap to be cold and stay cold which drastically slows down the ability of the RO system to filter water out of it. I ran into a bottle neck where there is more sap than I can keep up with concentrating so I needed to come up with something quickly!
![](https://i.nostr.build/B33D.jpg)
Ideally if the temperature of the sap is 77°f the filter will operate most effectively without damaging the RO membrane. Of course, my mind immediately turned to Bitcoin mining for the heating solution. What I came up with was an immersion system using the homebrew equipment I already had to heat the sap just before it entered the RO. This would allow the majority of the sap to stay cool keeping it from spoiling and still remove the most water possible.
![](https://i.nostr.build/e0Jz.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/aokZ.jpg)
The only thing I didn't have for the immersion system was the dielectric fluid. I had no idea where to find the proper fluid nor did it make sense to pay the high cost for it. The application for this system is very specific and I will only need it until April. I had been joking about using canola oil as dielectric fluid for almost a year but for this situation it seemed like the perfect fit. Canola oil is 70% cheaper than bitcool before shipping and was immediately available!
![](https://i.nostr.build/rDv2.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/J3qq.jpg)
Amazingly, I put everything together and it worked very well without major adjustments. I tip-toed the voltage and frequency of the single S9 hashboard up slowly to find the right balance in temperatures between the two fluid loops. Ultimately, I ended up with an overclocked board drawing over 600w! By the time I got the system setup and dialed in I was already half way through concentrating this collection of sap. The next collection will offer more concrete data on what this system is capable of. For now, even with the worst S9 board I have, I'm getting a 15% rebate on the total power usage of the whole process and it's definitely concentrating sap more quickly. All for ~$10 of canola oil... 👀

items.title: Trip Report: Paris
items.text:
Paris is known for its food and savoir vivre, the art of living your life. It comes as no surprise that the merchants I found accepting Bitcoin in Paris are all serving foods and drinks, and so this trip report is almost more of a food review than a Bitcoin review.

🧆In the hip 18th arrondissement lies Chez Ginette, a fairly typical cafe with its seats facing the trottoir, so Parisians can watch each other. The menu offers all the classic dishes you would expect from a place like this, but somehow lacks a theme or specialization. I order the greatest classic there is, the steak tartare. It comes préparé, meaning the raw egg is mixed in. It's definitely of high quality and I'm also happy about the pommes frites on the side. There is a "Bitcoin Lightning payments accepted" sticker on the door, and as I ask to pay with Bitcoin the waiter does not hesitate, although it takes him a while to get his colleague to come over with an orange point of sale terminal running the Swiss Bitcoin Pay app, built on BTCPay. The payment goes through almost instantly.

🍸Le Greffulhe is another cafe close to the opera and a high-end fashion district. As I arrive I mistake a man standing by the entrance for staff and ask him about Bitcoin paymnets. He says he would be surprised if they did, and indeed he is after we go inside together to ask the cashier. The cafe belongs to the same category as Chez Ginette, but the atmosphere feels very different, and although they do serve food, I never got the chance to try it during my two visits. Instead I had Aperol Spritz and Campari Soda, and payments went smoothly to the mobile phone of the cashier, also running Swiss Bitcoin Pay.

🍺Undoubtedly the heart of the Paris Bitcoin community is N'importe Quoi near Les Halles, somewhat in the geographical center of the city. The dive bar has the kind of anarchic and old-school feminist feel of a place that you almost expect to be taking Bitcoin. I'm here quite early and all by myself, and at first the bar tender denies my Bitcoin payment, saying "usually we do." Eventually she shows mercy with me and digs up the phone that has fallen somewhere behind the cash register, presumably only kept for the sole purpose of processing Bitcoin payments. The bar also uses Swiss Bitcoin Pay, and I'm quite pleased with how fast I can find a route to their node, and how I never paid more than 0.09% in fees, just a few sats.

🍝The Italian restaurant Costa d'Amalfi greets visitors with a warning: No Pizza. Connoisseurs will recognize this as a sign of quality, and indeed the family-run trattoria is exactly the kind of place you typically see accepting Bitcoin in Italy. Everything is well curated, the menu is short and specializes in one thing: truffle dishes. The owner comes over to talk to me about Bitcoin, telling me stories of his family and his Bitcoin story. He also uses the now familiar Swiss Bitcoin Pay and is quite happy with it.

🥮Located near Volontaires, an hommage to the volunteer soldiers of the French Revolution, is one of the areas of Paris known for their contemporary bohème lifestyle. Le Drapeau de la Fidélité fits it perfectly with its nondescript facade and carefully curated interior. There are plenty of books that make the restaurant feel more like a library, and they appear to have actually been read frequently. There are antiques, paintings, signed letters and a banner proclaiming a "Universal Humanist Capitalist Society" that I cannot find any other information about. The owner, a well-dressed older Vietnamese gentleman appears to run the tiny restaurant with its maybe 12 seats together with his son. The menu is short and the dishes simple and affordable. I order the porc caramélisé and pay a round 18,000 satoshi. The owner seems quite pleased with me paying with Bitcoin, which is always a great feeling when spending it. He uses Cake wallet, but doesn't know how to set an amount for his invoices. Also, his wallet is priced in USD, meaning I have to look up the rate on my end. As far as routing fees go, it's by far my most expensive payment at 0.3%.

🍷Near the Gare d'Austerlitz I visit La Brasserie L'Audièrnes. The area seems to be very popular with students, and everyone at the bar seems to be talking about AI, with many conversations in English. I order my drink at the bar and pay right away, but the cashier is hesitant to show me his wallet, and instead asks his colleague over. We navigate through the interface of some unfamiliar crypto wallet, and all we can find is an onchain address, which I pay to reluctantly.

I'm quite happy with my visit to Paris and especially the Bitcoin places that I found. I love the opportunity to find some random or hidden gems in the city that I would have never been able to visit if it weren't for Bitcoin. I love talking to the staff and the owners, there is always something to learn, and sometimes to teach, about how people are using Bitcoin. I also went to six other places, four of which were closed, and two of which no longer accept Bitcoin. At one of these places, the doors and cash register covered in Bitcoin stickers, I was practically laughed at for asking to pay with Bitcoin, before being asked to pay one Bitcoin to buy everyone a round. Finally one reason to implement BIP 177.

items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books I - III
items.text:
*Below I am starting the book club, as promised previously. It has probably taken longer than I originally led on. I expect that this can be forgiven. Whether you took up the challenge or not, there may be something for you in the following post. I have made an effort to give some original thoughts, followed by a character list and book summaries. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

# leading themes and ideas

* post-war society leads to excess and decay
* culture, values, family, country -- all need to be defended by their inheritors
* the most commonly held belief is not always the correct one

# Commentary

The first three books show how Telemachos has been living and responding to the apparent death of his father, Odysseus. Unbeknownst to Telemachos, his father is lost at sea, dealing with cyclops, and upsetting Poseidon in the meantime. With the help of other greek heroes (Achilles, Agememnon, Nestor, Menelaus etc.), Odysseus led the Achaeans to victory at the battle of Troy, and since then, things have not been going so well back home. This is the setup for the poem.

This is a story of what happens in the aftermath of war, when a great society produces heroes that defend its culture and norms against outsiders, and how, despite their victory on the battlefield, this same culture must be defended in their absence. This is seen at the outset, when the gods discuss what has become of the house of Atreus, whose son, Agememnon, finds himself the victim of Agisthos. The latter is eventually murdered by Agememnon's own son, Orestes, in an act of revenge for the murder of his father and the destruction of his household. Zeus laments the fact that, although they have brought this terrible fate upon themselves, men continue to hold Zeus to account. Wherever the fault lay, the poem tries to reckon with the phenomenon where society grows weak in the absence of the warriors who will defend their culture.

As the drama of the poem ensues, it is revealed how political infighting led the Achaeans to split up after Troy, leaving Agememnon and Odysseus away from their homeland. In the latter's absence, his wife Penelope and his son Telemachos have been left to defend what is left of his household. Suitors consume Odysseus' wealth, as they loiter, courting Penelope.

**So far, I have taken the following from the poem, summarized in a few sentences:**

* A great culture, such as the Greeks had, will produce great warriors, in whose absence its greatness will quickly fall to shambles.
* There will always be those willing to feast on the spoils bought by the sweat and blood of another person's brow
* Even when an entire population believe one thing, it may not be true. Truth is not easily discerned, but found out through persistence, struggle and adventure.

So, to you, reader of Epic poetry, I ask the question:

* Where do you see yourself on this cycle (i.e. good times --> weak men --> bad times --> strong men?)
* Is there an analogue in modern culture to the suitors feasting on Odysseus' wealth?

***

# Reading notes:

key characters

* Odysseys: a great warrior from Ithica. Never returned from the battle of Troy, in which he earned his stripes as a hero.
* Telemachos: the son of Odysseus.
* Penelope: the wife of Odysseus. Awaiting Odysseus' return.
* Suitors: men gathered in Ithica, enjoyers of Odysseus' house and belongings, as they vie for Penelope's hand in marriage.
* Zeus: Father of the gods. Feels let down by mortal men because of what happened in the aftermath of the battle of Troy concerning Agememnon.
* Aigisthos: killed Agememnon and married his wife. Is then killed by the latter's son, Orestes.
* Agememnon: in the aftermath of the battle of Troy, did not wish to sail home, for fear of displeasing Athena. He splits from Diomedes and Nestor, and stays in Troy
* Athena: Zeus' daughter. Favors Odysseus, intervenes for him so as not to see his house come into ruin
* Poseidon: god of the seas
* Mentes/Mentor: Athena in the form of a man, advises Telemachos in Ithica and in Pylos.
* Aigyptios: Wise councilman, blesses Telemachos
* Nestor: son of Neleus, king of Pylos.

# Book Summaries:

## Book I

> These men amuse themselves with music and song, freely, since they consume another’s wealth without repayment, one whose white bones are tumbling in the waves, or rotting in the rain on some far shore
> \--Mentes.

Zeus and Athena meet on Olympus. Lament Agememnon's murder and betrayal by Aigisthos. Athena descends from Olympus to intervene into the affairs of Telemachos, to keep him from a similar fate. His father, Odysseus, suffers the ire of Poseidon, who keeps him from returning home against the will of the other gods. Suitors, who think Odysseus is dead, harass Penelope and Telemachos, and take advantage of the latter's good manners. No one really knows whether Odysseus has died. Telemachos answers Mentes that he does not stop the suitors from courting his mother for the dread of not knowing what has come of his father. Before transforming into a bird to depart, Athena rouses Telemachos to gather the lords together and order them to stop, and moreover, that he should go out in search of his father.

## Book II

> ‘My lords, my Suitors, though Odysseus is dead and you are eager for me to marry, have patience till I complete this work, I do not want it wasted, this shroud for noble Laertes, ready for when pitiless death’s cruel end overtakes him: since I fear some Achaean woman of this land would blame me, if he who won great wealth lay there without a shroud.’
> \--Penelope

Telemachos assembles the lords of Ithica and makes his case, demanding that and end be put to the suitors' behavior. Antinous rebukes him, saying that Penelope has tricked them for the past three years, by saying she would choose a husband when the finishes weaving the shroud of Odysseus' father, Laertes, which she would work on during the day only to unravel the work she had completed under the darkness of night. Zeus sends an omen portending the destruction of the suitors. Athena again urges Telemachos to go in search of his father, provisions a ship and a crew for him, and even afflicts the suitors in Telemachos' home with drowsiness. Telemachos sets sail for Pylos in search of news of his father.

## Book III

Telemachos arrives at Pylos, where the people all pay sacrifice to the gods. Telemachos and Mentor make an offering to Poseidon, in Nestor's name. Telemachos appeals to Nestor, who also fought at Troy, to give news of what happened to Odysseus. He reports that the latter was caught in the middle of a feud between Menelaus, who wished to depart after the battle of Troy, and Agememnon, who feared the angering the gods, and wished to wait. Nestor and Odysseus went with Menelaus, leaving Agememnon behind. In a moment of hesitation, however, Odysseus turned back to join Agememnon. Nestor and Menelaus sail from Troy together and in the meantime, Aigisthos overtakes Agememnon, killing him and taking his wife for marriage. Nestor urges Telemachos to look on the heroism of Orestes, who took revenge against and murdered his father's murderer, Aigisthos. He tells Telemachos he needs to visit Menelaus for news of what came of Odysseus. Nestor offers Telemachos his men and ships, his hospitality, they sacrifice a heifer to Athena, and set off at dawn.

***

Why SoV -> MoE -> UoA for bitcoin
items.text:
I shared [an article](https://stacker.news/items/1582356/r/Undisciplined) about how things in the past have emerged as money. In brief the story is that commonly valued things (like salt, for instance) were easy to use for indirect exchange because almost everyone used them and that led to thinking in terms of how much you could exchange your salt for or how much salt you could attain for your goods (unit of account) and finally converting less storable goods into salt for future exchange (store of value).

The order seems to be different for bitcoin and people generally seem to accept that the order will be store of value (SoV), followed by medium of exchange (MoE), followed by unit of account (UoA). Why is that? I don't think anyone's written out the reasoning for ~bitcoin_beginners, although many of us probably have the same, or similar, understanding.

The short answer is that bitcoin obviously *can be* used for exchange, even if it isn't a prevailing MoE, and the hard supply cap makes it seem like a better money for savings than inflationary fiat currencies. In other words, people are taking it seriously as a money (even if only implicitly) and considering where it has the strongest advantage over other currencies.

That means the path to hyperbitcoinization will most likely look like

1. Commonly used as a store of value because fiat sucks hardest at that. As this progresses, the monetary premia of other assets (homes, fine art, precious metals, etc.) will be increasingly absorbed by bitcoin, resulting in much greater purchasing power.
2. Once bitcoin is the preferred savings technology, people will prefer receiving it in exchanges. That preference combined with bitcoin's lower transactions costs should lead to discounts for costumers willing to pay in bitcoin. That will further increase the purchasing power of bitcoin.
3. Only once bitcoin is commonly used for exchange will people do their accounting in bitcoin and denominate contracts in terms of bitcoin. Prior to that point, I suspect people will need to do mixed accounting where they keep track of their fiat and bitcoin income and expenses separately.

Is that roughly how everyone else sees events unfolding?

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: Why Were Victorian Elites so Effective? (Works in Progress Magazine, Sam Hughes)
items.text:
## Amazing (long) read, highly recommend

I like Works in Progress. *A lot*. It's a serious outlet for long-form journalism, and it (usually!) features writers whose minds are oriented correctly toward the future. (its editor-in-chief lost his mind during 'rona, so I've stayed away from reading/subscribing or even attempting to contribute... *but I'm often very tempted*)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160670)

## What's the Key For Success?

Work hard, long hours, education, 5am, cold plunges, diversity, pay your politicians well to avoid corruption *blah-blah*?

No, no:

> The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, **they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying.** They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

> the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance.

## In Defence of Debauchery

![](https://m.stacker.news/160674)

* **SCHOOLING:** while strict (early age, regulated times, single-sex away from family, corporal punishment), the values the English Victorian elite cultivated at boarding school were remarkably progressive: loyalty, internationalism, studies of the arts -- Latin and Ancient Greek --

Amazing:

> There was **resistance to the teaching of science, not because Victorians were hostile to science** in principle, but because they thought it **irrelevant to the kind of moral and cultural formation** that a school for gentlemen was supposed to provide.
> (By contrast, girls were not usually taught classics, meaning that, rather surprisingly, affluent Victorian girls generally followed a more modern curriculum than their brothers.)

While not obviously successful, it cultivated valuable skills:

> ...The most that can be said for Victorians’ classical education is perhaps that, like schooling in any difficult subject, it trained students in self-discipline, memorization, and applying rules.

And *this* we could definitely learn from today:

> Under such circumstances, it is perhaps unsurprising that the share of time spent in the classroom was relatively modest. At Rugby School, weeks were divided into three ‘full days’, three ‘half days’, and Sunday. On a full day, students spent about five hours in the classroom, compared with maybe two hours on a half day.  \[AND, importantly:] They also tended to be shorter than those of contemporary elite schools in France, Germany, or Italy, where the curriculum was normally more academically rigorous.

## "Victorians thought extremely highly of sports, believing that they instilled team spirit and endurance, fostered mutual loyalty, channeled energy and competitiveness, and taught men how to win and lose graciously."

One Loretto School headmaster described the school's priorities: **1) character, 2) physique,** 3) intelligence, 4) manners, 5) information. First time *brawns > brains, eh*

* **UNIVERSITIES**: Not much studying, plenty of "teambuilding"

I found *this* observation interesting:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160677)

> Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was not training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.

also:

> Fellowships were opened up to laymen in the later decades of the century, but **Oxford and Cambridge did not become world-leading research institutions until they were transformed by German scholars fleeing Nazism in the 1930s.** The dominance of Oxbridge in British culture was unusual: these institutions educated a much larger share of the elite than was the case for any two institutions in any other country

Fuck, these peeps just had *great* lives. (In some respects, Oxford life these days is very similar!)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160679)

* **ADULTHOOD**: Busy-busy-fucking busy bee... but not in the way you think

## "One virtue that upper-class Victorian education signally failed to inculcate was early rising. Although Victorian schoolboys and university students got up fairly early for chapel, the day of an upper-class Victorian adult started late."

Fuck *yeah!* Den loves victory https://stacker.news/items/1590741

The great statesmen and prime ministers back then "breakfasted at 9 am" or hosted a "social breakfast starting at 10.30 am (claret was served), continuing till about noon." **A-M-A-Z-I-N-G**

Also, not that different from today (minus the frock)

> general, however, Britain’s elites were slow to suburbanize, and in 1914 most still lived in centrally located row houses and walked to work. Every day a great herd of frock-coated men emerged from Belgravia and Mayfair and poured through Covent Garden to their offices in Parliament, Whitehall, the Inns of Court, and the City.

If you've noticed the drinking *at every goddamn meal*, you're not alone. It's pretty disturbing, an entire nation run by high-functioning alcoholics.

> The Victorians loved drinking and drank a lot by modern standards. Men drank more than women, but women drank a good deal too: one conduct guide[noted that](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/12426/pg12426-images.html)‘young ladies seldom drink more than three glasses of wine at dinner but married ladies, professional ladies, and those accustomed to society, and habits of affluence, will habitually take five or even six, whether in their own homes or at the tables of their friends’.

...and the partying, until the wee hours. Plus, for some odd reason Americans call this "Irish exit" (or French goodbye):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160682)

And they were hardly just for entertainment:

> the social events of the Victorian elite were notable for their lack of segregation by age or sex. A Society ball discharged the functions of both a teenage house party and a business networking convention: in fact, it*was* both a teenage house party and a business networking convention. \[...] Unmarried young people (and their unfortunate parents) might go to three or four balls per week, while other Society members would go to one or two. But the other nights were scarcely less busy. Opera, theatre and concerts were important, especially opening or gala nights.

Fuck, dudes kept busy.

> An MP might miss dinner for a late sitting of Parliament, but still drop into a soirée at 10.30pm, turn up to a supper party at 11.45pm, and then arrive at a ball at 1am. From February to July, the Victorian upper class led a remarkably nocturnal existence, with bedtimes in the small hours and the mornings something of a write-off.

## "All else being equal, rich and powerful Victorians must have been less productive for spending four hours a day in the office rather than twelve. But the creation of a single ruling *Gemeinschaft* may have had compensatory advantages."

Domestic and international (geo)political implications:

> This obviously had advantages for Britain. The elites of the American South had a very different identity to those of the North, and ultimately led the country into civil war. Spain, Italy and France suffered from incessant conflicts between urban bourgeois and rural nobility. Germany was riven with strife along geographical, religious, and class lines. **Some of these tensions existed in Britain, but except in Ireland, the elite finessed them peacefully.**

## "Would modern societies work better if their local and national government were conducted by a tight-knit community of extremely rich and successful people?"

The author thinks not... but a kid can dream, longing as we do for the best moment in (modern) Western civilization: the Victorian era.

items.title: How to Get People to Use Bitcoin
items.text:
For many years, I’ve been trying to figure out how to get bitcoin into people’s hands. Even long-time bitcoiners often don’t want to pay with bitcoin. At best, they slowly accumulate it, and they don’t really feel like they’re missing anything. They buy it on exchanges, pay fees, expose their personal information, and need a third party’s blessing for every transaction.

I sometimes hear people say that bitcoin doesn’t need anyone and that, on the contrary, we need bitcoin. I see it a little differently. To me, bitcoin is something like a living organism. I consider its creation to be an event almost as rare as the emergence of life itself. But for bitcoin to truly live and serve us as better money, I believe it needs users.

With every transaction, a new connection is created or an existing one is strengthened. Users gradually get better at securing their bitcoin, demand better tools, and bitcoin becomes more resilient.

That’s why I don’t think adoption is some kind of optional bonus.
**Adoption is a fundamental condition for bitcoin to actually be useful.**

## I tried various approaches

* I liked the idea of bringing bitcoin directly into Signal, for example: https://stacker.news/items/85702
  * But Signal still hasn’t added bitcoin support, and I’m afraid there simply isn’t enough incentive for them to do so anytime soon.
* Years ago, I also created an app that allowed people to load bitcoin onto an NFC card and pass it around much like cash: https://stacker.news/items/117623
  * Technically, it worked. But there wasn’t enough interest. It was a nice project, but it didn’t solve a real problem for people.
* Later, I also looked into why even bitcoiners themselves often don’t want to pay with bitcoin: https://stacker.news/items/210830

## It’s not enough to let merchants accept bitcoin

In the meantime, I onboarded dozens of businesses and bitcoiners locally.

Most of them were just isolated points on a map. A business started accepting bitcoin, but nobody actually paid with it. Eventually, the merchant forgot how to accept a bitcoin payment or what to do with the bitcoin they received.

It wasn’t until about a year ago that I managed to partially break through this problem.

I onboarded another business simply because we went there regularly. And to this day, every week we come there in a changing group of people, with everyone paying in bitcoin. https://stacker.news/items/1584550

![](https://m.stacker.news/159586)

The pub owner didn’t want bitcoin at all in the beginning. What matters to him is us as customers who come to his pub because of bitcoin. In the end, a merchant will accept pretty much any form of payment. What’s more important is finding people who are willing to pay with bitcoin.

Here, we use bitcoin also as a filter for finding interesting people. Anyone willing to pay with bitcoin is kind of open-minded, and it’s a pleasure to get to know them over a regular lunch.

## I don’t want to depend on a single app again

Over the years, I’ve recommended various wallets and tools to people. Some of them eventually disappeared.

The custodial version of Wallet of Satoshi, which was the most popular one, stopped working. Alza, the largest retailer in the Czech Republic and one of the first major merchants to accept bitcoin, started requiring additional administrative steps when paying with bitcoin. Qerko, which allowed bitcoin payments at around 1,000 businesses, removed bitcoin support.

At first, this was pretty discouraging. It was the end of 2025, and at the same time the price of bitcoin dropped significantly. I had to figure out what to do with the dozens of people I had introduced to a particular app, which was now no longer going to work for them.

I felt a little trapped. With every app, there was a risk that I would have to repeat the whole migration process again at any time.

But in January 2026, it also seemed to me that AI models had improved significantly, so I decided to try building my own wallet. One that I had been carrying around in my head for years.

## Linky

Linky is a bitcoin wallet and, at the same time, a communication layer for the people you want to use bitcoin with.

You can add your contacts, send them messages and bitcoin. You can pay any Lightning invoice. You can load bitcoin in the form of Cashu tokens onto an NFC card or send it to someone in a message — even to someone who doesn’t use Linky at all.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159587)

But I’m also trying to build a certain degree of antifragility into it.

From the beginning, I’ve been building Linky so that the app doesn’t depend on a particular operator. There are already other instances running on different domains. If my instance stopped working tomorrow, the network wouldn’t necessarily have to disappear with it.

We achieve this through a combination of three decentralized technologies:

* **Cashu** for bitcoin,
* **Nostr** for communication,
* **Evolu** for data storage.

We use several other interesting technologies as well, but I don’t want to get into the technical details here. There are now six other developers working on Linky. One of them is a close friend of mine who has been improving the app very intensively, primarily on the technical side.

What started as a funny vibecoded app is gradually becoming a serious project.

Around 250 people are currently testing Linky in the local group, and several hundred more users are using it.

## Individuals

People use Linky because they like it.

Thanks to its simplicity and steadily increasing reliability, it is gradually becoming the primary bitcoin wallet for many people.

**However, most people still don’t actually need a lightning wallet.** 😢

You can build a great wallet. You can onboard merchants. You can explain the benefits of bitcoin to people.
But if they have no reason to use bitcoin, all of those things will remain just flashes of activity.

## Proxy Payments

Recently, however, we managed to create a feature that I think can at least partially solve this problem. We call it **proxy payments**.

In the Czech Republic, people increasingly use QR codes for bank transfers. You can find them in online shops as well as physical stores.

For users, this is still somewhat less convenient than paying by card, but merchants love it because they don’t have to pay card-network fees.

Today, I can pay with bitcoin at any of these businesses. No fees and no KYC.

I scan the payment QR code using Linky - just as if I were paying a lightning invoice. Linky offers me the option to send the payment request to my contacts.

I select several friends and send them the offer.

Whoever accepts it first receives the payment details from the QR code. They pay the merchant from their bank account, and I send them sats in return.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159589)

## Does it worth the effort?

Maybe this sounds like a pointless detour. Why would I ask someone else to pay by bank transfer on my behalf when I could simply pay myself?

For me, it’s useful because I don’t have to hold fiat that is losing value.

For my friends, it’s useful because they don’t have to use an exchange, pay fees, or expose their personal information. They acquire bitcoin in an interactive way — usually in small amounts.

As a side benefit for everyone, there is the more abstract fact that you are building the bitcoin network and thereby helping ensure that you’ll be able to use bitcoin in the future as well.

To use proxy payments comfortably, you need roughly two or three people. Most payments are completed within two minutes. It’s not as direct or fast as paying by card, but it works surprisingly well.

Linky is showing people new ways to use bitcoin.

**Come help us test and build our shared bitcoin network. 🙏**

items.title: Bank Runs are Good, Actually: Death to the Central Banks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
ASTONISHING piece to see in regular financial press. *Maybe the tide is turning and the world is healing?*

![](https://m.stacker.news/159395)

The basic/most fundamental rationale for a central bank isn't financing the gov deficit (which they don't...*ish*) or set centralized interest rates, but to support commercial banks when faced with bank runs (=stand ready to lend against their assets, even if distressed, with newly created base money, so stave off the run.) The idea, from Francis Barings to Diamond\&Dybvig's [Nobel Prize](https://stacker.news/items/1583458?commentId=1583534) winning article, is that depositors are fickle and might/will run on perfectly healthy banks *and* that such runs cause real damage to the economy (*and* might spread through the banking system like wildfire and we all collapse into Great Depression 2.0).
*That's everything that's wrong with monetary economics and politics around central banks in one sentence...*

***

The authors of the paper Nangle discusses here used the Chronicling America project, scanned newspapers, then...

> they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159396)

> According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

This is incredible. Specifically, — and I'm sparing you a deep dive into debates in financial history and monetary economics here — a big rationale for *why central banks must exist* is **to prevent bad types of bank runs.**

Running a bank means it has to shed assets, assets that aren't "finished," or turned into workable projects and thus liqudity, yet. (That's sort of the purpuse of a bank: to *liquify* illiquid assets, hold the maturity and duration mismatch in the meantime.)  Selling these assets quickly means taking (large) haircuts on book value, meaning a random run on a healthy bank can destroy projects or at least turn the bank itself bankrupt -- destroying customer relatioships and disrupting the bank-money-level money supply etc etc. 
**That's all unnecessary, and a benevolent central bank/observer can improve upon the state of the world by injecting more money and support the healthy bank.**

## ...except, depositors don't run on healthy banks!

That's what this beautiful history and database shows. Somehow, depositors (in aggregate) are clever enough to sniff out when something is wrong *and not* structurally/mindlessly/sunspot-style make erratic and concentrated mistakes.

If you scratch [the lender or last resort literature a little](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/when-did-the-bank-of-england-become-a-lender-of-last-resort/), you find that it's a good, disciplining market mechanism for depositors to run on banks. Here's a schematic:

* if bank is healthy and other bankers know it, then the bank can source enough liquidity from them ("recycling" deposits), against a very minimal short-term expense. **No problem, no negative outcome, no need for lender of last resort** 
* if the bank is unhealthy and the other bankers know it, they won't lend to it and it will fail, *and it will be a good thing!* Bankers taking bad risks or making bad investments should fail, like every other business in a market economy.
* if the bank is healthy, but the **other bankers don't know it** *and so refuse to lend*, that's when a lender of last resort needs to step in and save the day. By supplying that extra liquidity it can stave off the damaging run and everyone is better off for it.

Here's the best short article/overview I've ever seen on this (by [George Kaufman, for econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/BankRuns.html)):

![](https://m.stacker.news/159394)

---

The literature on bank runs and central banks is basically an exercise in showing **whether or not the central bank knows about the true state of a given bank better than other bankers do.**

When central banks *also* had prudential obligation, by chance some of its workers would have recently audited and inspected private information for that bank, meaning it's quite plausible that central bankers *do* have some insider information here that they can act on. (Nowadays that function is usually separated to another agency, thus the argument is practically quite moot.)

But... If historically and practically depositors are good enough in aggregate to sniff out what's wrong, there's no *need* for a central bank to intervene and override their market choice.

Bank runs are bad for local economies

> ...only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

...in which case there is **a real economic loss that we want/need someone to carry** — not paper over and pretend it's not there. (\_cough\_, Bitfinex...)

***

Told yah:

> Surely **the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy?** Apparently not.

> Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

and:

> Out of **3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934**, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”. Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to **non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”**
> one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

*Even that*, the depositors sniffed out. Amazing.

***

All "pretty interesting" says Nangle, understating the explosive result.

> the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Yes. This evidence shows/weighs heavy that lender of last resort is a defunct and unnecessary function — liable to abuse, nepotism, and trigger-happy rulers, not actually saving a banking system that needs it

## Runs are good. Banks should fail more. And lender of last resort is an unnecessary function

items.title: Book Review: Broken Money and the Way Out, PART 1: MONEY (the Invity Team)
items.text:
TAKEAWAY NUMERO UNO: If there's a successful book titled *Broken Money*, you DO NOT title your own marketing pamphlet/e-book style "Broken Money" as well.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159635)

***

I spent some time today looking through the Invity people's fintech offering. We met at BTCHEL, where they launched/announced some cool banking features for us Europooreans. https://stacker.news/items/1580878, https://stacker.news/items/1581849 https://stacker.news/items/1585380

Particularly, quite convenient **auto-stacking, payment cards with bitcoin/stablecoins,** and **juicy-af cashback** on every spend. (Up to stupidly [low maximums](https://www.invity.io/personal-accounts), it turns out -.-)

This is all very tempting, and Den is a sucker for a good sats deal (*aren't we all?!*), so what does a bookish nerd do?

## Download and read the free e-book, of course!

***

It's from their educational platform, Invity Academy (as if we didn't have enough educational outlets...):

> It is meant for people who know Bitcoin from headlines and debates, but never got an answer to the most important question: why did it come about at all, and what problem does it solve?
> We start with money itself — how it came about, how it works today, and why so many people feel that something about it „broke“. Only once we understand the problem does it make sense to talk about a solution.

Oh, turns out this is *really* for Mr. Den. Let's dig in.

*Blah-blah-blah*, money's three functions, and various properties (ignoring, for now, Erik Yakes' *7th Property*, **Immutability** https://stacker.news/items/1572208)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159636)

...gold, commodity money, stock-to-flows. Alright, amazing. State intervention, Roman coins.

## "If you were born after 1971, you live in a historical anomaly"

Pretty neat account:

* 1870-1914: Classical gold standard
* 1933: gold banned
* 1971 Nixon Shock

They definitely overdo the importance of 1971, a mere formality in a world already addicted to fiat and money printing. (1914 is a more important civilizational cutoff.)

Cool, but graphs like these are pretty boring. A *dollar*, like *a* bitcoin, is not a meaningful economic unit; nobody (rationally) cares about *a* dollar, but the relationship between what they have and earn to what they invest and consume. e.g., https://stacker.news/items/737272, https://stacker.news/items/1578595

![](https://m.stacker.news/159637)

> 1913 the Fed, 1933 the ban on holding gold, 1944 Bretton Woods, 1971 the Nixon Shock — four steps from hard money to fiat. → Since 1971 no currency in the world has been backed by anything tangible

VERY nice

![](https://m.stacker.news/159638)

> How money is actually created today
> → The vast majority of the money in your account was created by commercial banks, not the state.
> → New money comes into being at the moment of a loan. When you repay the loan, the money disappears.
> → QE lets a central bank create money in the order of trillions within weeks.
> → The M2 money supply grows substantially faster than real output.

## AMAZINGLY witty: "Money-supply inflation is the cause, price inflation is the symptom."

![](https://m.stacker.news/159639)

Here's a scary graph, but of course *financing conditions* matters too: An average interest rate for mortgages in Czechia was about [7% in 2000](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Average-mortgage-loan-interest-rate-1995-2005_fig7_24080862); [below 5%](https://www.globalpropertyguide.com/europe/czech-republic/mortgage-interest-rate) in 2025.

## Inflation as a silent tax

![](https://m.stacker.news/159641)

> Modern central banking is often defended with the argument that it stimulates the economy and creates jobs. Even if we take that at face value, we must at the same time see the flip side: the money a central bank creates does not arrive for everyone at once. It travels a predictable path that structurally favours one group over another.

VERY eloquent and punchy.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159640)

> At the end of the pipe stand

* **The fixed-wage employee**: the wage is usually adjusted only with a delay, and not by the full extent of inflation.
* **The pensioner** — the pension is indexed once a year, slowly.
* **The young family** without assets — they own no assets to rise in value, yet pay higher prices for food, energy, rent.
  -**The saver** on a savings account — the interest does not cover the loss of purchasing power

These things are conditional and not *obviously* and *always* the case; boomers in America enjoy pretty competitive COLAs; interest rates on savings accounts in Iceland are ~halfway between CPI and monetary expansion. With bond prices collapsing, rates on (high-yield, short-term) bank accounts like those at fintechs are bound to rise explosively. https://stacker.news/items/1578425

***

## NOTHING STOPS THIS LYN ALDEN TRAIN

Yeah, dudes didn't just *borrow* Lyn's title; they take her fiscal framework too: there's no way back/out from governments' profligacy and debt-to-GDP ratios. America just *cannot* outgrow [40trn in debt](https://stacker.news/items/1554591) (...unless we scalp the boomers https://stacker.news/items/1468968, you know the drill.)

> An economic term returning to the debate in recent years is fiscal dominance. It means a state of affairs where the state’s budgetary situation is so strained that the central bank cannot run an independent policy. Lyn Alden describes that the United States entered this situation around 2022. The interest cost on US federal debt exceeded the defence budget in 2024 — and that is a defence budget which is itself larger than the budgets of the next ten largest countries combined.

The financial FIXES that used to work:

* The **60/40 portfolio**: yeah, it's entirely dead. Also, bonds don't provide *neither* uncorrelated returns, nor inflation-adjusted returns at all.
* savings account: guaranteed losses. Czech republic example is \~4% interest on savings, 2.5% official inflation... BUT tax the nominal return 15% *and* assets like flats and properties rose *way more* than 1-2%.
* New fixes?

> Holding large cash in the bank is, over the long run, a strategy by which the state really taxes your purchasing power. Diversification remains valuable, but it must include assets that respond to monetary degradation (hard assets). Gold passed the test of 5,000 years. Neutral, apolitical, independent of the banking system. Bitcoin is new — it has 15 years behind it. But if its properties are confirmed, it offers everything gold does, and more: portability, verifiability, divisibility and neutrality in a form gold can never have.

...in PART 2, dudes move on to the orange solution: \_bitcoin\_, woop woop!

items.text:
Yeah, we all know the reason climate change ~~activism~~ delusion doesn't have a higher uptick is... *toxic masculinity*!

**oh lord.**

![](https://m.stacker.news/160711)

> **If you are a man who cares about climate change, are you a bit of a dweeb? Put another way, if a man says global warming is rubbish, does he seem more manly**? In my 15 years of writing about climate change, these are not questions I have considered before. But I have begun to do so since coming across research that suggests a lot of men brush off the climate problem for fear of seeming too feminine.

## why do studies and polls across the world consistently show that men care less about global warming than women?

It's all just socialization and sexism.

> Some studies suggest that men feel they have more to lose from policies to fight climate change. Others conclude it is because women are socialised to care more about things like the environment. But researchers who focus on socialisation tend to look at it from the perspective of the women being socialised.

*alternative candidates*: women constitutionally less fit for public convos (unlikely), women too high in neuroticism/liable to catastrophizing (plausible), women harder time thinking through trade-offs/op cost (maybe); men more attuned to the real professions that make society function (definitely).

> Using data from the US, and a long-running survey of more than 40,000 people across Europe, he showed that men who say they want to save the planet are perceived to be more warm and caring. In keeping with this finding, he also showed that men who are strongly concerned about maintaining their sense of manhood express less concern about the climate problem and say they feel less responsibility for managing it.

## GIEF MANHOOD!

> A study of more than 9,000 scientists in 115 countries published this week shows that those who believe technology will largely solve the climate problem are 23 per cent less likely to go on a climate march, sign a petition or take similar civic actions, compared with scientists who lack such faith. The techno-optimists are also 18 per cent less likely to make big lifestyle changes to cut carbon. In other words, many personal views matter, even for experts.

Being attuned to tech (fixed) make you less activist-worthy... sooo, having a male-oriented mind must be bad/sexist.

## "But Haselhuhn’s work does raise a question about the best way to sell the need for climate action, especially to men."

lol, yeah... because it's all a matter of *marketing*. No substance problem, no economic consideration, no green-stuff-was-just-low-interest-rate-phenomenon.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160712)

oh, and just FYI... if you object to climate "facts," you're not just in denial: **you're suffering from SOLUTION AVERSION.** *Fucksake, give me a break*.

> It doesn’t help to spout scientific facts to show why \[your climate-denying uncle, a man\*\*] is wrong, Hayhoe told a recent FT conference. That’s because the real issue here is not science denial but solution aversion, or concern that climate policies will clash with a person’s identity, ideology or ideas about a better world.

> **Because it’s unpleasant to say openly that you don’t want to fix a serious problem, people use so-called motivated reasoning to find grounds** for why climate change cannot be real or serious. In other words, they process information in ways that align with what they already believe or want, rather than with objective evidence.

Or... maybe, just *maybe*, there's a deeper, higher-order, system-levels thinking required... trading off one thing for another, or (peeeerhaps??) it's not as bad as the green activists \~say\~ scream loudly on the tube, covered in pig's blood...

Ah fuck. Some people's (dare I say, *women?!*) intellectual echo chambers and cognitive deficiencies are, eh, shocking.

> Happily, Hayhoe says, the same uncle’s views can reverse completely if he buys solar panels that save him money or does something else that improves his own circumstances as well as the climate. There is a message here for **those of us who rightly worry about warming temperatures.** Scientific facts really matter, as does the health of the environment. But there will be times when the best thing you can do for the planet is not talk about it at all.

items.title: Why Are Bond Yields Suddenly so High?! (FT, Chris Giles)
items.text:
*Great question, few good answers.*

![](https://m.stacker.news/160553)

"The big question is why yields have risen so much."

* Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability?
* Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth?
* Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders?
* Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation?
* Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back?
* Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility?
* Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Chris Giles goes through some of these and provide some decent rebuttals.

> Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were [three broad reasons](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20260916.pdf) at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.
> The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

## "The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling"

![](https://m.stacker.news/160554)

Seems obvious, but I'm still a little stuck on the **transmission mechanism** : there's no reason, in principle, that wars or even oil price shocks ought to result in higher yields

The analogy being the 1970 had a few other critical components: **labor unions aggressively striking** for higher wages, setting off a price-wage push; and **central banks eager to accommodate** the real-cost push with new money.

There's no risk for the former, as labor unions worldwide (minus the Nordics, but they're pretty meek here) are a ghost of their former self. And the latter is entirely under our own control; central bankers can decide not to accommodate oil price increases (or actively crush demand... ), thus gaining credibility for their monetary policy *and* an indication of how independent they are from the fiscal authorities.

I guess, then, the bond market is pragmatic and saying "Fat chance, Den; dream the fuck on — dudes will print."

STILL, I find it kind of weird, then, to jump past the intermediate steps and conclude that wars (or oil prices) cause inflation and thus yields.  **No, (central) *banks printing money* cause inflation, *always and everywhere*.** For immediate analogy: Planes don't crash because of gravity, even though of course gravity is involved and 'ultimately' the cause.

> There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift.

Another commonly quipped reason is that AI has unleashed *massive* productivity gains that are about to swamp GDP numbers -- thus rates ought to go up (via the real economy). So far, only a single quarter of a sliver of such indications. AND:

> anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

Also, this investment boom is not *that* visible (outside specific sectors):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160560)

The other option is that capital is *expensive* now, with AI debt issuance swallowing up all the air in the room, *lol mixing metaphors*:

> Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

> there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros.

## "No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default."

eeeh, cute. *Maybe look further afield than your standard sources, fren*?!

***

Archive still messing w us... lmk if you want the full article -- lots of good graphs in there.

items.title: What is your favorite paradox?
items.text:
Mathematical, logical, philosophical, economical, or otherwise:  what is your favorite paradox?

Mine is the Ship of Theseus.  It goes something like this:

> Every year the Athenians sail the Ship of Theseus to the island of Delos to worship their God Apollo.  After every voyage, any planks that had been worn out from the voyage are replaced by new planks.  After many years, none of the original planks remain.  What's more, it's discovered that a shipwright had been quietly saving and restoring the discarded planks and he used them to rebuild the original ship plank for plank.  Which ship is the Ship of Theseus?

The reason I like this one is because it asks about the meaning of identity, and the continuity of it.  It's inspired a lot of fiction, like Star Trek's transporter episodes, The Prestige, and Klara and the Sun.  It's also not an abstract logical paradox - it is easily envisioned and explained in real world terms, but it doesn't admit a clean solution.
