items.title: Latest Strikes #42 - October 12th-18th 2026
items.text:
Welcome to Latest Strikes, your weekly report of the latest Lightning-related news. In today's issue, we cover Lightning Labs' new scaling proposition, an interesting cross-layer routing protocol, and more!

![](https://m.stacker.news/162823)

## Lightning Labs Unveils LayerTree

Lightning Labs [unveiled](https://x.com/lightning/status/2110812651882217677) [LayerTree](https://layertree.tech/), a new scaling protocol with 2 core characteristics:

* many (thousands to tens of thousands) users share one single on-chain UTXO, while retaining unilateral exit rights;
* a user leaving the tree requires only one on-chain transaction, independent of the number of users in the tree.

To simultaneously realize these 2 often contradictory properties, LayerTree leverages an off-chain Merkle-sum tree to keep a record of balances, and a set of yet-to-be-activated opcodes (basically, covenants). The exact set of opcodes depends on the targeted implementation (or maybe the other way around), with the minimal version requiring `OP_CAT` and `OP_TWEAKADD`.

[Paper](https://layertree.tech/paper/main.pdf) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1596351/r/fanis)

## Lexe Connect

Lexe unveiled [Lexe Connect](https://docs.lexe.tech/lexeconnect/), a protocol and [specification](https://github.com/lexe-app/lexe-connect) that lets apps request scoped access to your Lexe node. As a reminder, [Lexe](https://www.lexe.app/) is a self-custodial Lightning wallet featuring an LSP, where the node runs in a remote [TEE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trusted_execution_environment) (Trusted Execution Environment) rather than on your phone[^1].

Such a feature makes a lot of sense in Lexe, since it means you can have one always-online Lightning node and connect your apps to it, rather than having one wallet, often custodial, baked into each app. All this with no channel management, since the LSP takes care of that.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594737/r/fanis) | [YouTube Demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bh951sWxP3Q)

## Landfall

Speaking of Lexe, Vincenzo Palazzo [unveiled](https://x.com/PalazzoVincenzo/status/2107915680465219605) [Landfall](https://github.com/vincenzopalazzo/landfall), an app (web, desktop and agent CLI) aimed at making it easier for Ocean miners to receive their payouts in Lightning. As Palazzo explains, one of the hiccups is that Ocean requires the miner to sign a message using [BIP322](https://bips.xyz/322), which is not often offered by Lightning wallets. Ocean miners hence [need](https://ocean.xyz/docs/lightning#:~:text=A%20Lightning%20node%20supporting%20BOLT12) to find a Lightning wallet that supports Bolt12 and a way to sign a message with the same seed used by the wallet.

Landfall does precisely that: it generates a new seed, displays it to the user for backup, and uses it to both create a new Lexe wallet (and node)[^2] and sign the requested message. What was previously quite the headache becomes only a few steps, easy to follow for anyone who has already set up a wallet before.

Disclaimer: as Palazzo puts it, "Landfall is a showcase, not a production wallet".

## Cassis

[Cassis](https://cassis.cash/) is an interesting formalization (as a protocol) of the idea that multiple Bitcoin layers can be composed in a single payment, as long as each of them supports HTLCs. While such composition is already routinely used today, it's often (always?) limited to one transition: paying a Lightning wallet from a Cashu mint, doing a swap between Liquid and Lightning, depositing on an Ark with a Lightning payment, etc. There might be multiple hops involved in the Lightning part of the payment itself, but there's only one additional hop before or after this Lightning part. While it's theoretically possible to bridge across even more layers in a single payment **atomically**, it becomes a manual process rather than something that happens behind the scenes when the user hits "Pay"[^3].

Cassis simplifies all that with a routing protocol. Nodes advertise which networks they support through Nostr (e.g. a specific Fedimint instance, Lightning, Liquid, a specific Ark, on-chain Bitcoin, etc.) and can be reached through [iroh](https://www.iroh.computer/) when someone wants to route a payment through them. This is basically onion routing, but instead of routing nodes passing down and peeling an onion, the payer's wallet coordinates the whole payment by pinging each node when it's their turn to forward the payment[^4]. So not onion routing at all. Should we call it Cassis Routing?

I think it's great to have a formalized protocol implementing and coordinating multi-layer hops. Of course, it's still very early, but I'll be very curious to see if it catches on!

[Delving Bitcoin Post](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/cassis-a-new-simple-scheme-for-generic-multi-layer-multi-hop-htlc-routing/2952) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1591643/r/fanis)

## Zeus Release

Zeus v13.2.3 was [released](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/releases/tag/v13.2.3), fixing bugs and bringing the usual amount of improvements and security hardenings. A few editorial picks:

* the embedded LDK node was bumped to version 0.2.7 of rust-lightning, bringing in LDK's October 1st [security release](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-38-39-40-41#ldk-release);
* for receiving, Zeus [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4673) checks that the invoice wrapped by the LSP matches the one it initially generated, before showing it to the user;
* LNURL-Auth [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4576) checks that the callback host matches the signing domain, preventing a class of man-in-the-middle attack where a malicious party could pose as the website the user wants to connect to, and intercept the valid login to access the victim's account on the website themselves;
* Zeus can [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4658) parse (and thus, pay) [BIP353](https://bips.xyz/353) records that contain more than one payment method, e.g. a silent payment address and a Bolt12 Offer. Neat!
* and many, many more things. Check the release notes for more details.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594119/r/fanis)

## Quick Strikes

* Alby Hub [v1.24.3](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.3) was released, bringing back on-chain <> Lightning swaps, and many improvements and bug fixes. Note that this is not the latest, since [v1.24.4](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.4) was released yesterday;
* the ([sunset](https://x.com/nixbitcoinorg/status/2087880779892158679)) nix-bitcoin project was [rebooted](https://x.com/PavolRusnak/status/2110300699070537897) as [bitcoinix](https://github.com/bitcoinix/bitcoinix) by a group of developers, including Trezor co-founder Pavol Rusnak;
* [Lightning in a Jar](https://lightninginajar.xyz/) (LiJ) is a browser on-chain and Lightning wallet, powered by [LDK](https://lightningdevkit.org/) compiled to WebAssembly. The team is also building [LIJOX](https://lightninginajar.xyz/#lijox), an open list of LSPs that any LND operator can join by running an adapter on top of their node. They're [looking for](https://stacker.news/items/1596404/r/fanis) such operators to give it a try, as well as eyes on their LDK patch set.
* [lxdev](https://lx.dev/) (we covered their dark pools prototype [here](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-30#quick-strikes)) announced [Zark](https://hackmd.io/@januszgrze/HJlHensozl), a privacy-focused blinded statechain protocol that basically tries to improve on [MercuryLayer](https://mercurylayer.com/)'s design by adding zero-knowledge to further reduce the (already small) level of information leak when transacting on the statechain. It's definitely great to see the privacy-focused approach of statechains make a comeback!

***

That's it for last week! Thank you so much for reading this far, and until next week!

[^1]: Basically [Phoenix](https://phoenix.acinq.co/) in the cloud. Which makes sense for a bird.

[^2]: This leverages a yet-unreleased feature of Lexe that lets users bring their own seed when provisioning a new node.

[^3]: For example, you could initiate an Ark onboarding, take the on-chain address returned by the server, use it as the destination of a Lightning-to-bitcoin atomic swap, and pay the Lightning invoice returned by the swap service from your Cashu wallet.

[^4]: More precisely, the payer's wallet first builds a route, and sends a `prepare` message (through iroh) to each node in that path. Each of them can review the terms (amount, fees, destination, involved networks, etc.) and accept or reject. Once all accept, the payer's wallet locks the route and initiates the payment, sending an HTLC to the first node, and sending them an `execute` message, which contains details about the incoming HTLC. The first routing node proceeds to forward the payment to the next node, using another HTLC, and reports back to the payer. The payer then uses the information from this response to send an `execute` message to the next node, with details about the incoming HTLC from the first routing node, and so on.

items.title: [REVIEW] Cryptonomicon by Neal Stephenson
items.text:
The book's ending is all wrong. It's really where the story is just about to get going, but when you've already subjected your readers to 1100 pages, you're options are limited. In this case, our heroes are about to launch a new cryptography-based digital money sans government support.

> "Electronic cash from the Crypt. Anonymous. Untraceable. And untaxable."
>
> Doug's regained his composure now, and is back to belly laughs. "What will that buy me? Pictures of naked girls on the World Wide Web?"
>
> "Soon enough, it'll buy you anything that money *can* buy," Tom says.

This is the story I wanted in *Cryptonomicon*, instead we get a whole lot about code-breaking and WWII and the lives of Gen X-ers. Gripping and enjoyable in that many of the heroes are Walter Whites in their own domains, but ultimately, not the cyberpunk epic I was hoping for.

*Cryptonomicon* was published in 1999 and you get glimmers of the crypto wars, the promise that, armed with heavy-duty math and personal computers, the common man could stand up to Big Brother. Plus, even at that early stage of the internet, Stephenson clearly gets it:

> One has to assume this is an attempt to launch some sort of philosophical debate. Arguing with anonymous strangers on the Internet is a sucker's game because they almost always turn out to be -- or to be indistinguishable from -- self-righteous sixteen-year-olds possessing infinite amounts of free time.

Yet, if you are gonna write a book about a book called the Cryptonomicon, I expect a little more math magic (there's plenty of math in \*Cryptonomicon\*, just all of it is rather mechanical). I want to see the sly roundabout power of cryptography at work defending the little guy, but most of what Stephenson is concerned with here is breaking codes, not making them. There is a cool little bit of code with a deck of cards by Bruce Schneier, but otherwise it's all cracking keys.

I did dig the way Stephenson juxtaposed the people who use cryptography with the people who create cryptography: the big moral there is that codes are only so strong as the people who send them. He makes the hacker approach to cryptography very attractive. But that's the problem: we don't to see the hackers really launch their project.

> Basically, the assayer's scale was the exchange point -- the place where the mineral, this dirt from the ground, became money that would be recognized as such in any bank or marketplace in the world, from San Francisco to London to Beijing. Because of the nerd's special knowledge, he could put his imprimatur on dirt and make it money. Just like we have the power to turn bits into money.

The nerds and their special knowledge -- first of gold, later of math, and networking -- can turn bits into money. But we never get to see them actually do it, and the story ends, rather depressingly if you ask me, with a kind of ho-hum reveal about just how their are going to do it. \*Cryptonomicon\* could have been Icarus, but instead it's just another story about a bank.

We continue the braincell-killing exercise */slash/* Den self-flagellation that is reading *The Natural Dividend*. https://stacker.news/items/1515430, https://stacker.news/items/1565551, https://stacker.news/items/1588944

In this episode, the authors -- successful Norwegian academics whose cognitive deficiencies are on full display throughout the book -- get *shockingly close* to understanding **subjective value theory**. *And then, very predictably, botch the entire exercise*.

## We also learn a little bit about their biases and where this shit is coming from

***

First, the asshats give a pair of nonsensical conditions — incorrect even according to their own frameworks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160346)

Because (a) fails by implication in their view, since *nature* was made by nobody... But how could value then ever flow back to the "maker"? They already raged against God (https://stacker.news/items/1588944?commentId=1588955), and Darwin doesn't have a bank account. In the real world of sane economics, the value *does* flow back to the producers, since the producer isn't God or nature but the guy who extracted the thing (oil, metals, wind, fish etc etc). The eeeentreeeepreeeeneeeeur.

(If you think this error still **just hinges on market "value,"** you're right... *but please just wait up; don't beat me to it...)*

Second, nature is now alive and well, *acting* in Mises' framework:

> We have already recognized that nature is not of our making; it exists independently of our efforts. This section aims to demonstrate that **this independent nature can create value**, which can be subsequently commodified and sold on the market. (39)

Yeah, no. Talk about misunderstanding value... 

Cmon, fuck heads, just crack open an economics textbook — any of them! — and check subjective valuation and labor theory of value stuff (even *that* defunct and outdated worldview would have rescued them from such errors).

**Next page, they get *stunningly close* to getting it:**

![](https://m.stacker.news/160347)

Again, the "productive forces of nature itself" is shockingly anthropomorphic... Yeah, sure, nature is alive and demands a paycheck for its hard work crushing organic matter or hurling gale-force winds at you.

Plus, of course "the political authorities that regulate access to nature" are the default owners (https://stacker.news/items/1588944). *ugh*.

## "Imagine a pool of oil lying deep below the ocean bottom"

...ok, ok, ok! *Now we're getting somewhere!!* I'm excited!

> ... This oil, lying untouched in the raw, **has no market value;** it only has the potential to become valuable.

Yes yes yes, okay. Good! And how? Who brings the valueless thing alive/to market and makes it valuable, what about the physical nature of the oil shifts between the *ocean floor* and the *refinery*?? Aah, yes, you guys are so close!

> ... The same can be said of the labour and capital inputs we attribute to the \[owner]: without access to the raw materials (provided by nature), **labour and capital inputs are worthless**

Aaah, no: *that's an error*. Labour and (almost all) capital have secondary, alternative use! They are and can be deployed elsewhere. Their "reservation price" isn't zero, like the oil at the bottom of the sea nobody can do anything with.

Oooh look at that "brought together" idea... I wonder, the *government* as an entrepreneur, making things happen... *Where have I heard that before??*

***

## "In making this argument, we hope to avoid the quagmire that is the valuation problem in contemporary economics"

Oh boy. There's no *valuation problem* and certain not in *contemporary* economics. This was all worked out largely a hundred years ago, between the marginal revolution (https://stacker.news/items/1471628) and subjective value, the socialist calculation debate and the Cambridge capital controversy. And sidestepping "value" is precisely the core error of your whole book!

...but let's check that sneaky footnote (fn10) and see what's up:

It's **Mariana Mazzucato**, the author of [*The Entrepreneurial State*](https://link.amazon/B07wuXz9P)!! And here, the authors cited her follow-up book, *The Value of Everything*... *in addition to* an overview book *by two Marxists* about a supposed value conflict, from 1982. (Like cooome the fuck oooon!!). As if Ms Mazzucato is anything but a fringe, irrelevant, non-representational figure in "contemporary economics." As if MARXIST AUTHORS have anything meaningful or important to say about CONTEMPORARY ECONOMICS. 

My. Fucking. God. I ask, as one of my professors at Oxford liked to quip in seminars:

## Who on Earth was the peer reviewer for this?!

items.title: Against Supplements (Works in Progress mag, Ben Southwood)
items.text:
Aaah, this is the kind of progress (https://stacker.news/items/1599758) I can get behind: **via negativa; addition by subtraction** https://stacker.news/items/1540851

Dude comes to terms with his extensive and unfortunately mostly useless supplementation regimen.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162920)

He *had* a pretty good test/method:

> I reasoned that though we can’t be absolutely sure, a supplement was, on balance, likely worth taking if three things held. First, we have a plausible evolutionary story about how we originally evolved in an environment with more of it, and our modern diets do not. Second, there is a logical, not obviously disputed, story about how it works. Third, the balance of evidence suggests that consuming the nutrient at least correlates with good health, and ideally well-designed trials show that it actually causes good health.

His problem?

> I didn’t really believe in all the supplements I was taking – I just treasured the esoteric dietary knowledge, like a kind of modern-day druid

\= *It was all confirmation bias*

> **food obsessiveness**. I’m afraid that I was a pathologically, distressingly fussy child who would eat only a handful of plain foods. As a teenager, I forwent artificial colorings and flavorings completely, to an extent that made people think (rightly) that I was a freak. For years, I ate only during a six-hour window between 2pm and 8pm. At other times, I have obsessively counted calories, or completely avoided carbs. Currently, I just eat a lot of fiber. **I follow dietary fads like I am constantly switching religions**

Also, there's a "science" problem at the heart of this:

> My feeling had always been that we could still draw conclusions if we had a big enough pile of papers. But now I have come to believe that **something like 90 percent of research is nearly valueless.**

## "Another perhaps equally big problem is that most science is nearly useless."

Loving the game, not the play

> This complexity was a great deal of what made the whole thing so enjoyable, akin to being into a fandom like Warhammer with a lot of lore, or a sport like baseball with very rich statistics.

> This isn’t to say that there are never beneficial supplements for normal omnivores, but I am now suitably chastened.

Yes, at 66° N **we stopped making vitamin D from the admittedly scant sunlight about a month ago**. So yeah, I supplement that, for sure: usually via cod liver oil (or more pleasantly via gummy bears). I also occasionally take some magnesium — I fall in and out of this practice — again on some pretty flimsy evidence that it's good for muscle recovery, sleep, and most importantly, preventing migraines.

I refer you to the main rule above: science knows almost nothing about the world, and certainly nutrition.

items.title: Loyalty/Rewards and Other Monetary Scams: The Points Guy (Net Interest)
items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: How do you deal with your children’s friends whom you don’t like?
items.text:
I am aware that trying to forbid a friendship is impossible and can lead to greater defiance and damage the bond not to mention that what is forbidden often becomes all the more tempting. At the same time, it cannot be denied that some friendships do not constitute good company. Admittedly, this is a very broad generalization; everything depends on our personal values, and such situations become even more complex during adolescence.

A little context of what is happening with my daughter: She has a friend (both are 9 years old) whom she met at school during the last school year, and it just so happens that we live pretty close to each other. The girl comes over to our house, my daughter has been to her house, I take them to the park—everything seemed normal. However, I’ve noticed that this girl tells a lot of lies and always uses phrases like "don't tell your mom/my mom," which I suppose is relatively normal at that age, but I don't know. My daughter told me that the girl said to her, "I can have a boyfriend as long as we don't do 'things'." I played dumb and asked my daughter what she meant by "things," and my daughter said, "I don't know, she didn't tell me."

What has disturbed me the most so far—and what I felt requires the utmost caution—is that she told my daughter to bruise her own arms, and when I asked her what happened, to say "nothing." But when my husband arrived, she was supposed to start shaking, crying, and blame him for the bruises. She also told her to look up phrases on YouTube to make her parents argue. The purpose of this plan was because my daughter was upset with her dad, and her friend came up with a revenge plot. I don't know about you, but to me, it seems horrible, and I cannot comprehend how a little girl can scheme a plan like that.

My daughter did not self-harm; quite the opposite, she told me what her friend had suggested that very same day. I didn't scold her, and I didn't judge her; I just listened and explained the risks involved in hurting oneself and falsely incriminating someone. I thanked her for being honest with me. After this, I didn't speak with the girl's mother, but I did speak with the school psychologist so they could handle it. My daughter and her friend are no longer in the same classroom—they are in different shifts now—and currently, they only see each other at my house or when I take them to the park.


I know I can't put my daughter in a bubble and control everything that happens around her, but I must give her the tools so she knows how to defend herself and recognize people and situations she shouldn't get into because they put her physical and moral integrity at risk. And of course, to let her know that she will always have my support. It sounds very easy, but it is much more complicated than that.

items.title: You don't have to mine Bitcoin
items.text:
Had a photo shoot today with a really awesome woman, and we ended up talking about all sorts of things, including Bitcoin.

I asked her where she was in her Bitcoin journey, and she told me she’d been curious about it a few years ago but never got into it because she didn’t know how to mine Bitcoin.

I thought that was interesting. She didn’t realize you don’t have to mine Bitcoin to acquire it. You can buy it, earn it, or accept it as payment.

I’d never heard that as a reason for someone not getting into Bitcoin before. Has anyone else?

She was really fascinated once we talked more about how it works and how to get started. Now she wants to sit down with me another time so I can walk her through it in more detail.

items.title: Latest Strikes #42 - October 12th-18th 2026
items.text:
Welcome to Latest Strikes, your weekly report of the latest Lightning-related news. In today's issue, we cover Lightning Labs' new scaling proposition, an interesting cross-layer routing protocol, and more!

![](https://m.stacker.news/162823)

## Lightning Labs Unveils LayerTree

Lightning Labs [unveiled](https://x.com/lightning/status/2110812651882217677) [LayerTree](https://layertree.tech/), a new scaling protocol with 2 core characteristics:

* many (thousands to tens of thousands) users share one single on-chain UTXO, while retaining unilateral exit rights;
* a user leaving the tree requires only one on-chain transaction, independent of the number of users in the tree.

To simultaneously realize these 2 often contradictory properties, LayerTree leverages an off-chain Merkle-sum tree to keep a record of balances, and a set of yet-to-be-activated opcodes (basically, covenants). The exact set of opcodes depends on the targeted implementation (or maybe the other way around), with the minimal version requiring `OP_CAT` and `OP_TWEAKADD`.

[Paper](https://layertree.tech/paper/main.pdf) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1596351/r/fanis)

## Lexe Connect

Lexe unveiled [Lexe Connect](https://docs.lexe.tech/lexeconnect/), a protocol and [specification](https://github.com/lexe-app/lexe-connect) that lets apps request scoped access to your Lexe node. As a reminder, [Lexe](https://www.lexe.app/) is a self-custodial Lightning wallet featuring an LSP, where the node runs in a remote [TEE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trusted_execution_environment) (Trusted Execution Environment) rather than on your phone[^1].

Such a feature makes a lot of sense in Lexe, since it means you can have one always-online Lightning node and connect your apps to it, rather than having one wallet, often custodial, baked into each app. All this with no channel management, since the LSP takes care of that.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594737/r/fanis) | [YouTube Demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bh951sWxP3Q)

## Landfall

Speaking of Lexe, Vincenzo Palazzo [unveiled](https://x.com/PalazzoVincenzo/status/2107915680465219605) [Landfall](https://github.com/vincenzopalazzo/landfall), an app (web, desktop and agent CLI) aimed at making it easier for Ocean miners to receive their payouts in Lightning. As Palazzo explains, one of the hiccups is that Ocean requires the miner to sign a message using [BIP322](https://bips.xyz/322), which is not often offered by Lightning wallets. Ocean miners hence [need](https://ocean.xyz/docs/lightning#:~:text=A%20Lightning%20node%20supporting%20BOLT12) to find a Lightning wallet that supports Bolt12 and a way to sign a message with the same seed used by the wallet.

Landfall does precisely that: it generates a new seed, displays it to the user for backup, and uses it to both create a new Lexe wallet (and node)[^2] and sign the requested message. What was previously quite the headache becomes only a few steps, easy to follow for anyone who has already set up a wallet before.

Disclaimer: as Palazzo puts it, "Landfall is a showcase, not a production wallet".

## Cassis

[Cassis](https://cassis.cash/) is an interesting formalization (as a protocol) of the idea that multiple Bitcoin layers can be composed in a single payment, as long as each of them supports HTLCs. While such composition is already routinely used today, it's often (always?) limited to one transition: paying a Lightning wallet from a Cashu mint, doing a swap between Liquid and Lightning, depositing on an Ark with a Lightning payment, etc. There might be multiple hops involved in the Lightning part of the payment itself, but there's only one additional hop before or after this Lightning part. While it's theoretically possible to bridge across even more layers in a single payment **atomically**, it becomes a manual process rather than something that happens behind the scenes when the user hits "Pay"[^3].

Cassis simplifies all that with a routing protocol. Nodes advertise which networks they support through Nostr (e.g. a specific Fedimint instance, Lightning, Liquid, a specific Ark, on-chain Bitcoin, etc.) and can be reached through [iroh](https://www.iroh.computer/) when someone wants to route a payment through them. This is basically onion routing, but instead of routing nodes passing down and peeling an onion, the payer's wallet coordinates the whole payment by pinging each node when it's their turn to forward the payment[^4]. So not onion routing at all. Should we call it Cassis Routing?

I think it's great to have a formalized protocol implementing and coordinating multi-layer hops. Of course, it's still very early, but I'll be very curious to see if it catches on!

[Delving Bitcoin Post](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/cassis-a-new-simple-scheme-for-generic-multi-layer-multi-hop-htlc-routing/2952) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1591643/r/fanis)

## Zeus Release

Zeus v13.2.3 was [released](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/releases/tag/v13.2.3), fixing bugs and bringing the usual amount of improvements and security hardenings. A few editorial picks:

* the embedded LDK node was bumped to version 0.2.7 of rust-lightning, bringing in LDK's October 1st [security release](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-38-39-40-41#ldk-release);
* for receiving, Zeus [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4673) checks that the invoice wrapped by the LSP matches the one it initially generated, before showing it to the user;
* LNURL-Auth [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4576) checks that the callback host matches the signing domain, preventing a class of man-in-the-middle attack where a malicious party could pose as the website the user wants to connect to, and intercept the valid login to access the victim's account on the website themselves;
* Zeus can [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4658) parse (and thus, pay) [BIP353](https://bips.xyz/353) records that contain more than one payment method, e.g. a silent payment address and a Bolt12 Offer. Neat!
* and many, many more things. Check the release notes for more details.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594119/r/fanis)

## Quick Strikes

* Alby Hub [v1.24.3](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.3) was released, bringing back on-chain <> Lightning swaps, and many improvements and bug fixes. Note that this is not the latest, since [v1.24.4](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.4) was released yesterday;
* the ([sunset](https://x.com/nixbitcoinorg/status/2087880779892158679)) nix-bitcoin project was [rebooted](https://x.com/PavolRusnak/status/2110300699070537897) as [bitcoinix](https://github.com/bitcoinix/bitcoinix) by a group of developers, including Trezor co-founder Pavol Rusnak;
* [Lightning in a Jar](https://lightninginajar.xyz/) (LiJ) is a browser on-chain and Lightning wallet, powered by [LDK](https://lightningdevkit.org/) compiled to WebAssembly. The team is also building [LIJOX](https://lightninginajar.xyz/#lijox), an open list of LSPs that any LND operator can join by running an adapter on top of their node. They're [looking for](https://stacker.news/items/1596404/r/fanis) such operators to give it a try, as well as eyes on their LDK patch set.
* [lxdev](https://lx.dev/) (we covered their dark pools prototype [here](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-30#quick-strikes)) announced [Zark](https://hackmd.io/@januszgrze/HJlHensozl), a privacy-focused blinded statechain protocol that basically tries to improve on [MercuryLayer](https://mercurylayer.com/)'s design by adding zero-knowledge to further reduce the (already small) level of information leak when transacting on the statechain. It's definitely great to see the privacy-focused approach of statechains make a comeback!

***

That's it for last week! Thank you so much for reading this far, and until next week!

[^1]: Basically [Phoenix](https://phoenix.acinq.co/) in the cloud. Which makes sense for a bird.

[^2]: This leverages a yet-unreleased feature of Lexe that lets users bring their own seed when provisioning a new node.

[^3]: For example, you could initiate an Ark onboarding, take the on-chain address returned by the server, use it as the destination of a Lightning-to-bitcoin atomic swap, and pay the Lightning invoice returned by the swap service from your Cashu wallet.

[^4]: More precisely, the payer's wallet first builds a route, and sends a `prepare` message (through iroh) to each node in that path. Each of them can review the terms (amount, fees, destination, involved networks, etc.) and accept or reject. Once all accept, the payer's wallet locks the route and initiates the payment, sending an HTLC to the first node, and sending them an `execute` message, which contains details about the incoming HTLC. The first routing node proceeds to forward the payment to the next node, using another HTLC, and reports back to the payer. The payer then uses the information from this response to send an `execute` message to the next node, with details about the incoming HTLC from the first routing node, and so on.

items.title: Off-wallet: opensource hardware wallet for Gameboy Color
items.text:
This is totally vibecoded, but the concept is interesting:

Run your wallet on hardware that was built before Bitcoin came out and that doesn't have wifi or bluetooth or a radio of any sort. Also it has a kind of nice plausible deniability to it.

> The private key is generated on the console from 128 coin flips you watch land, and it never leaves the cartridge. It signs its own spends: BIP-341 key-path taproot, BIP-340 Schnorr, computed on a 4 MHz 8-bit CPU, and the signed transaction leaves the console the only way anything can -- through the screen, as QR codes or as hex you can read.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162691)

It seems like you have to tell the signer about transactions you want to sign by hand:

> The coins you own are typed in by hand from a block explorer, because that is the only way facts about the chain can reach a machine with no antenna.

In general the flow is interesting:

|                                                                                                            |                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ![The professor](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/02-professor.png)             | **Talk to the professor.** Every line of dialogue, every screen and every character lives in [`content/story.txt`](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/blob/main/content/story.txt), not in the C.                        |
| ![Choosing a starter](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/03-starter.png)          | **Pick a starter.** Bitcoin is the only one that hatched in this world. The other two refuse to be selected.                                                                                                                  |
| ![Choosing an egg](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/04-egg.png)                 | **Pick an egg.** SWIFT is one standalone key, backed up as a WIF string, and hatches in about 70 seconds. ANCIENT is a 12-word BIP-39 seed phrase at `m/86'/0'/0'/0/0`, restorable in any wallet, and takes about 19 minutes. |
| ![Flipping coins for entropy](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/05-flipping.png) | **Flip your key.** One press, one coin flip, straight onto the grid. 128 flips, 128 bits. The counters show heads, tails and the longest run of the same result.                                                              |
| ![All 128 flips taken](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/06-flips-done.png)      | **Check the tally, then keep it.** 128 fair flips land near 64/64 with no run much past eight. `SELECT` throws the sequence away and starts again.                                                                            |
| ![Deriving the key](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/07-hatching.png)           | **Wait for the hatch.** The bar is driven from the VBlank interrupt, so the screen keeps moving while the CPU grinds through the elliptic curve.                                                                              |
| ![The wallet menu](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/09-wallet-menu.png)         | **The wallet.** Address, QR code, your UTXO list and balance, the secret, the raw output key, and save-to-cartridge.                                                                                                          |
| ![The taproot address](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/10-address.png)         | **A real `bc1p…` address.** 62 characters of bech32m over four lines.                                                                                                                                                         |
| ![The QR code](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/11-receive-qr.png)              | **Receive by QR.** Version 3, error-correction level L, 29×29 modules at three pixels each. A phone reads it straight off the screen.                                                                                         |
| ![The UTXO list](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/12-utxos.png)                 | **Your own ledger.** Transaction id, output index and amount, typed in from a block explorer, kept in cartridge SRAM with its own checksum.                                                                                   |

items.title: How to Invest Like the University Endowments (WSJ, Specer Jakab)
items.text:
The big/fancy universities and their endowments get a lot of investing attention.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162881)

Two major reasons:

1. they have access and connections (and attract the best of the best via extremely high-paid staff) that you and I don't.
2. they follow the YALE MODEL from the 1980s by David Swensen: underweight bonds and harvest illiquidity, basically.

Still, there are some differences.

> The Massachusetts Institute of Technology [says that its massive endowment](https://news.mit.edu/2026/mit-releases-financials-and-endowment-figures-1002), managed by executives who earn more than the university’s president, **earned 10.3% during its fiscal year ended in June**. That’s less than half of what an S\&P 500 index fund earned.

Not that impressive. Weird that the MIT team hadn't done better. Problem? Didn't have SpaceX pre-IPO...

> MIT’s results are more surprising during a tech boom that it might seem uniquely equipped to harness. Harvard and Stanford’s endowments, which held big stakes) i**n SpaceX acquired before its IPO, jumped 27.1% and 31.7%**, respectively. The University of North Carolina, which had more than a tenth of its endowment in that stock, did even better.

Great [Musk](https://stacker.news/items/1600448)-ivite payoff to the "live a little" crowd (https://stacker.news/items/1600985)

> As uplifting as one-year moonshots are, big college endowments offer tuition-free lessons these days about how *not* to invest. Special access to mostly so-so but costly private equity, hedge and venture-capital funds has seen their returns lag what mom and pop investors could have made over the past decade.

## Swansen "could take a very long view, and illiquid investments were cheaper back then."

NOW?

Not so much. Private credit sumbling... everybody wants a piece of the pre-IPO AI hassle. The Robinhoods of the world, whose Venture Fund with early access in some of these AIs, "sports a 3.1% expense ratio, 100 times the cost of an S\&P 500 index fund..." Then again, it's in *their* interest to open *that* bit up to their business... and the Trump Admin have voiced special accounts or bitcoin or private markets in e.g., 401(k)s. **These are weird times.**

> \[Investing veteran Richard] Ennis writes that endowment managers "mostly operate as if nothing has changed" since Swensen's heyday. Allocating 60% to alternatives costs them about 3% annually, or about what Robinhood charges, according to his math.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162883)

***

items.title: Anthropic's Gigantic Net Loss, and Other Cool Stories About Fake Finance
items.text:
This *will* have a Saylor connection (https://stacker.news/items/1600946), *bear* with me...

![](https://m.stacker.news/162864)

So then Mr. Levine goes through three hypothetical scenarios that transfer ownership/economic rights between a company and an outside investor:

1. **Sell 10% of a 10m company on Jan 1.** When Dec 31, company is worth 100m, that outside investor turned 1m into 10m, and the company's original owners have equity worth 90m. The *company* didn't change, but the distribution of owners did (100% of 10m vs 90% of 100m). *This does not hit the company's income statement, obviously*.
2. Company **promises to deliver 10% of stocks to outside investor on Dec 31, against 1m fronted right now.** It's worth 10m on Jan 1 and 100m on Dec 31. It's in some sense a *loan*... but

> For most of the year, the company didn’t have that outside shareholder; instead what it had was, effectively, a bet against its stock. Still, this is basically the same as the first scenario; it’s just a delayed issuance of stock. \[...] **It’s not paying the investor $10 million in cash; it’s just giving the investor the agreed-upon amount of stock.**

3. Company worth 10m on Jan 1, **gets 1m today against a *promise* of cash-settled 10% of company value** at the end of the year:

> Dec. 31, the company is worth $100 million, and it pays the investor 10% of that, $10 million, in cash. The investor has made a $9 million profit. Has the company made a $9 million *loss*? Definitely, right? That’s a real cash payment; the company *just* made a cash-settled bet against its stock, and lost. Pretty clearly this reduces its net income.

> Companies do raise money by promising to issue stock in the future: They sell convertible bonds or warrants, giving the buyer the option to get stock in the future. If a company sells a $1,000 bond that converts into 50 shares of stock when the stock is at $20, and then the stock goes to $50, then the bond is worth $2,500. The bondholder has made $1,500. Has the company lost $1,500? Does it have to reduce its net income by $1,500?

Kind of.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162869)

...and now, for Anthropic's gigantic 80bn net loss for H1:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162873)

.... so, what's up with STRC and MSTR and Saylor? When company goes up in value and fuels itself, perpetual motion machine style, by a) constant inflows via repeated promises to outside investor, and b) when that doesn't work -- which is quite often -- dilute common shareholders by \~1-2% per week... *do you end up with net losses in the company?!*

Of course not accounting wise, but what company management is doing is repeatedly hurling over (new) equity to outside investors for an ever-appreciating company.

**Not sure that's a great idea, browskie.**

items.title: Against Supplements (Works in Progress mag, Ben Southwood)
items.text:
Aaah, this is the kind of progress (https://stacker.news/items/1599758) I can get behind: **via negativa; addition by subtraction** https://stacker.news/items/1540851

Dude comes to terms with his extensive and unfortunately mostly useless supplementation regimen.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162920)

He *had* a pretty good test/method:

> I reasoned that though we can’t be absolutely sure, a supplement was, on balance, likely worth taking if three things held. First, we have a plausible evolutionary story about how we originally evolved in an environment with more of it, and our modern diets do not. Second, there is a logical, not obviously disputed, story about how it works. Third, the balance of evidence suggests that consuming the nutrient at least correlates with good health, and ideally well-designed trials show that it actually causes good health.

His problem?

> I didn’t really believe in all the supplements I was taking – I just treasured the esoteric dietary knowledge, like a kind of modern-day druid

\= *It was all confirmation bias*

> **food obsessiveness**. I’m afraid that I was a pathologically, distressingly fussy child who would eat only a handful of plain foods. As a teenager, I forwent artificial colorings and flavorings completely, to an extent that made people think (rightly) that I was a freak. For years, I ate only during a six-hour window between 2pm and 8pm. At other times, I have obsessively counted calories, or completely avoided carbs. Currently, I just eat a lot of fiber. **I follow dietary fads like I am constantly switching religions**

Also, there's a "science" problem at the heart of this:

> My feeling had always been that we could still draw conclusions if we had a big enough pile of papers. But now I have come to believe that **something like 90 percent of research is nearly valueless.**

## "Another perhaps equally big problem is that most science is nearly useless."

Loving the game, not the play

> This complexity was a great deal of what made the whole thing so enjoyable, akin to being into a fandom like Warhammer with a lot of lore, or a sport like baseball with very rich statistics.

> This isn’t to say that there are never beneficial supplements for normal omnivores, but I am now suitably chastened.

Yes, at 66° N **we stopped making vitamin D from the admittedly scant sunlight about a month ago**. So yeah, I supplement that, for sure: usually via cod liver oil (or more pleasantly via gummy bears). I also occasionally take some magnesium — I fall in and out of this practice — again on some pretty flimsy evidence that it's good for muscle recovery, sleep, and most importantly, preventing migraines.

I refer you to the main rule above: science knows almost nothing about the world, and certainly nutrition.

items.title: Loyalty/Rewards and Other Monetary Scams: The Points Guy (Net Interest)
items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: How do you deal with your children’s friends whom you don’t like?
items.text:
I am aware that trying to forbid a friendship is impossible and can lead to greater defiance and damage the bond not to mention that what is forbidden often becomes all the more tempting. At the same time, it cannot be denied that some friendships do not constitute good company. Admittedly, this is a very broad generalization; everything depends on our personal values, and such situations become even more complex during adolescence.

A little context of what is happening with my daughter: She has a friend (both are 9 years old) whom she met at school during the last school year, and it just so happens that we live pretty close to each other. The girl comes over to our house, my daughter has been to her house, I take them to the park—everything seemed normal. However, I’ve noticed that this girl tells a lot of lies and always uses phrases like "don't tell your mom/my mom," which I suppose is relatively normal at that age, but I don't know. My daughter told me that the girl said to her, "I can have a boyfriend as long as we don't do 'things'." I played dumb and asked my daughter what she meant by "things," and my daughter said, "I don't know, she didn't tell me."

What has disturbed me the most so far—and what I felt requires the utmost caution—is that she told my daughter to bruise her own arms, and when I asked her what happened, to say "nothing." But when my husband arrived, she was supposed to start shaking, crying, and blame him for the bruises. She also told her to look up phrases on YouTube to make her parents argue. The purpose of this plan was because my daughter was upset with her dad, and her friend came up with a revenge plot. I don't know about you, but to me, it seems horrible, and I cannot comprehend how a little girl can scheme a plan like that.

My daughter did not self-harm; quite the opposite, she told me what her friend had suggested that very same day. I didn't scold her, and I didn't judge her; I just listened and explained the risks involved in hurting oneself and falsely incriminating someone. I thanked her for being honest with me. After this, I didn't speak with the girl's mother, but I did speak with the school psychologist so they could handle it. My daughter and her friend are no longer in the same classroom—they are in different shifts now—and currently, they only see each other at my house or when I take them to the park.


I know I can't put my daughter in a bubble and control everything that happens around her, but I must give her the tools so she knows how to defend herself and recognize people and situations she shouldn't get into because they put her physical and moral integrity at risk. And of course, to let her know that she will always have my support. It sounds very easy, but it is much more complicated than that.

items.title: You don't have to mine Bitcoin
items.text:
Had a photo shoot today with a really awesome woman, and we ended up talking about all sorts of things, including Bitcoin.

I asked her where she was in her Bitcoin journey, and she told me she’d been curious about it a few years ago but never got into it because she didn’t know how to mine Bitcoin.

I thought that was interesting. She didn’t realize you don’t have to mine Bitcoin to acquire it. You can buy it, earn it, or accept it as payment.

I’d never heard that as a reason for someone not getting into Bitcoin before. Has anyone else?

She was really fascinated once we talked more about how it works and how to get started. Now she wants to sit down with me another time so I can walk her through it in more detail.

items.title: Latest Strikes #42 - October 12th-18th 2026
items.text:
Welcome to Latest Strikes, your weekly report of the latest Lightning-related news. In today's issue, we cover Lightning Labs' new scaling proposition, an interesting cross-layer routing protocol, and more!

![](https://m.stacker.news/162823)

## Lightning Labs Unveils LayerTree

Lightning Labs [unveiled](https://x.com/lightning/status/2110812651882217677) [LayerTree](https://layertree.tech/), a new scaling protocol with 2 core characteristics:

* many (thousands to tens of thousands) users share one single on-chain UTXO, while retaining unilateral exit rights;
* a user leaving the tree requires only one on-chain transaction, independent of the number of users in the tree.

To simultaneously realize these 2 often contradictory properties, LayerTree leverages an off-chain Merkle-sum tree to keep a record of balances, and a set of yet-to-be-activated opcodes (basically, covenants). The exact set of opcodes depends on the targeted implementation (or maybe the other way around), with the minimal version requiring `OP_CAT` and `OP_TWEAKADD`.

[Paper](https://layertree.tech/paper/main.pdf) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1596351/r/fanis)

## Lexe Connect

Lexe unveiled [Lexe Connect](https://docs.lexe.tech/lexeconnect/), a protocol and [specification](https://github.com/lexe-app/lexe-connect) that lets apps request scoped access to your Lexe node. As a reminder, [Lexe](https://www.lexe.app/) is a self-custodial Lightning wallet featuring an LSP, where the node runs in a remote [TEE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trusted_execution_environment) (Trusted Execution Environment) rather than on your phone[^1].

Such a feature makes a lot of sense in Lexe, since it means you can have one always-online Lightning node and connect your apps to it, rather than having one wallet, often custodial, baked into each app. All this with no channel management, since the LSP takes care of that.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594737/r/fanis) | [YouTube Demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bh951sWxP3Q)

## Landfall

Speaking of Lexe, Vincenzo Palazzo [unveiled](https://x.com/PalazzoVincenzo/status/2107915680465219605) [Landfall](https://github.com/vincenzopalazzo/landfall), an app (web, desktop and agent CLI) aimed at making it easier for Ocean miners to receive their payouts in Lightning. As Palazzo explains, one of the hiccups is that Ocean requires the miner to sign a message using [BIP322](https://bips.xyz/322), which is not often offered by Lightning wallets. Ocean miners hence [need](https://ocean.xyz/docs/lightning#:~:text=A%20Lightning%20node%20supporting%20BOLT12) to find a Lightning wallet that supports Bolt12 and a way to sign a message with the same seed used by the wallet.

Landfall does precisely that: it generates a new seed, displays it to the user for backup, and uses it to both create a new Lexe wallet (and node)[^2] and sign the requested message. What was previously quite the headache becomes only a few steps, easy to follow for anyone who has already set up a wallet before.

Disclaimer: as Palazzo puts it, "Landfall is a showcase, not a production wallet".

## Cassis

[Cassis](https://cassis.cash/) is an interesting formalization (as a protocol) of the idea that multiple Bitcoin layers can be composed in a single payment, as long as each of them supports HTLCs. While such composition is already routinely used today, it's often (always?) limited to one transition: paying a Lightning wallet from a Cashu mint, doing a swap between Liquid and Lightning, depositing on an Ark with a Lightning payment, etc. There might be multiple hops involved in the Lightning part of the payment itself, but there's only one additional hop before or after this Lightning part. While it's theoretically possible to bridge across even more layers in a single payment **atomically**, it becomes a manual process rather than something that happens behind the scenes when the user hits "Pay"[^3].

Cassis simplifies all that with a routing protocol. Nodes advertise which networks they support through Nostr (e.g. a specific Fedimint instance, Lightning, Liquid, a specific Ark, on-chain Bitcoin, etc.) and can be reached through [iroh](https://www.iroh.computer/) when someone wants to route a payment through them. This is basically onion routing, but instead of routing nodes passing down and peeling an onion, the payer's wallet coordinates the whole payment by pinging each node when it's their turn to forward the payment[^4]. So not onion routing at all. Should we call it Cassis Routing?

I think it's great to have a formalized protocol implementing and coordinating multi-layer hops. Of course, it's still very early, but I'll be very curious to see if it catches on!

[Delving Bitcoin Post](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/cassis-a-new-simple-scheme-for-generic-multi-layer-multi-hop-htlc-routing/2952) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1591643/r/fanis)

## Zeus Release

Zeus v13.2.3 was [released](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/releases/tag/v13.2.3), fixing bugs and bringing the usual amount of improvements and security hardenings. A few editorial picks:

* the embedded LDK node was bumped to version 0.2.7 of rust-lightning, bringing in LDK's October 1st [security release](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-38-39-40-41#ldk-release);
* for receiving, Zeus [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4673) checks that the invoice wrapped by the LSP matches the one it initially generated, before showing it to the user;
* LNURL-Auth [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4576) checks that the callback host matches the signing domain, preventing a class of man-in-the-middle attack where a malicious party could pose as the website the user wants to connect to, and intercept the valid login to access the victim's account on the website themselves;
* Zeus can [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4658) parse (and thus, pay) [BIP353](https://bips.xyz/353) records that contain more than one payment method, e.g. a silent payment address and a Bolt12 Offer. Neat!
* and many, many more things. Check the release notes for more details.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594119/r/fanis)

## Quick Strikes

* Alby Hub [v1.24.3](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.3) was released, bringing back on-chain <> Lightning swaps, and many improvements and bug fixes. Note that this is not the latest, since [v1.24.4](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.4) was released yesterday;
* the ([sunset](https://x.com/nixbitcoinorg/status/2087880779892158679)) nix-bitcoin project was [rebooted](https://x.com/PavolRusnak/status/2110300699070537897) as [bitcoinix](https://github.com/bitcoinix/bitcoinix) by a group of developers, including Trezor co-founder Pavol Rusnak;
* [Lightning in a Jar](https://lightninginajar.xyz/) (LiJ) is a browser on-chain and Lightning wallet, powered by [LDK](https://lightningdevkit.org/) compiled to WebAssembly. The team is also building [LIJOX](https://lightninginajar.xyz/#lijox), an open list of LSPs that any LND operator can join by running an adapter on top of their node. They're [looking for](https://stacker.news/items/1596404/r/fanis) such operators to give it a try, as well as eyes on their LDK patch set.
* [lxdev](https://lx.dev/) (we covered their dark pools prototype [here](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-30#quick-strikes)) announced [Zark](https://hackmd.io/@januszgrze/HJlHensozl), a privacy-focused blinded statechain protocol that basically tries to improve on [MercuryLayer](https://mercurylayer.com/)'s design by adding zero-knowledge to further reduce the (already small) level of information leak when transacting on the statechain. It's definitely great to see the privacy-focused approach of statechains make a comeback!

***

That's it for last week! Thank you so much for reading this far, and until next week!

[^1]: Basically [Phoenix](https://phoenix.acinq.co/) in the cloud. Which makes sense for a bird.

[^2]: This leverages a yet-unreleased feature of Lexe that lets users bring their own seed when provisioning a new node.

[^3]: For example, you could initiate an Ark onboarding, take the on-chain address returned by the server, use it as the destination of a Lightning-to-bitcoin atomic swap, and pay the Lightning invoice returned by the swap service from your Cashu wallet.

[^4]: More precisely, the payer's wallet first builds a route, and sends a `prepare` message (through iroh) to each node in that path. Each of them can review the terms (amount, fees, destination, involved networks, etc.) and accept or reject. Once all accept, the payer's wallet locks the route and initiates the payment, sending an HTLC to the first node, and sending them an `execute` message, which contains details about the incoming HTLC. The first routing node proceeds to forward the payment to the next node, using another HTLC, and reports back to the payer. The payer then uses the information from this response to send an `execute` message to the next node, with details about the incoming HTLC from the first routing node, and so on.
