items.title: Off-wallet: opensource hardware wallet for Gameboy Color
items.text:
This is totally vibecoded, but the concept is interesting:

Run your wallet on hardware that was built before Bitcoin came out and that doesn't have wifi or bluetooth or a radio of any sort. Also it has a kind of nice plausible deniability to it.

> The private key is generated on the console from 128 coin flips you watch land, and it never leaves the cartridge. It signs its own spends: BIP-341 key-path taproot, BIP-340 Schnorr, computed on a 4 MHz 8-bit CPU, and the signed transaction leaves the console the only way anything can -- through the screen, as QR codes or as hex you can read.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162691)

It seems like you have to tell the signer about transactions you want to sign by hand:

> The coins you own are typed in by hand from a block explorer, because that is the only way facts about the chain can reach a machine with no antenna.

In general the flow is interesting:

|                                                                                                            |                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ![The professor](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/02-professor.png)             | **Talk to the professor.** Every line of dialogue, every screen and every character lives in [`content/story.txt`](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/blob/main/content/story.txt), not in the C.                        |
| ![Choosing a starter](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/03-starter.png)          | **Pick a starter.** Bitcoin is the only one that hatched in this world. The other two refuse to be selected.                                                                                                                  |
| ![Choosing an egg](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/04-egg.png)                 | **Pick an egg.** SWIFT is one standalone key, backed up as a WIF string, and hatches in about 70 seconds. ANCIENT is a 12-word BIP-39 seed phrase at `m/86'/0'/0'/0/0`, restorable in any wallet, and takes about 19 minutes. |
| ![Flipping coins for entropy](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/05-flipping.png) | **Flip your key.** One press, one coin flip, straight onto the grid. 128 flips, 128 bits. The counters show heads, tails and the longest run of the same result.                                                              |
| ![All 128 flips taken](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/06-flips-done.png)      | **Check the tally, then keep it.** 128 fair flips land near 64/64 with no run much past eight. `SELECT` throws the sequence away and starts again.                                                                            |
| ![Deriving the key](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/07-hatching.png)           | **Wait for the hatch.** The bar is driven from the VBlank interrupt, so the screen keeps moving while the CPU grinds through the elliptic curve.                                                                              |
| ![The wallet menu](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/09-wallet-menu.png)         | **The wallet.** Address, QR code, your UTXO list and balance, the secret, the raw output key, and save-to-cartridge.                                                                                                          |
| ![The taproot address](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/10-address.png)         | **A real `bc1p…` address.** 62 characters of bech32m over four lines.                                                                                                                                                         |
| ![The QR code](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/11-receive-qr.png)              | **Receive by QR.** Version 3, error-correction level L, 29×29 modules at three pixels each. A phone reads it straight off the screen.                                                                                         |
| ![The UTXO list](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/12-utxos.png)                 | **Your own ledger.** Transaction id, output index and amount, typed in from a block explorer, kept in cartridge SRAM with its own checksum.                                                                                   |

items.title: How to Invest Like the University Endowments (WSJ, Specer Jakab)
items.text:
The big/fancy universities and their endowments get a lot of investing attention.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162881)

Two major reasons:

1. they have access and connections (and attract the best of the best via extremely high-paid staff) that you and I don't.
2. they follow the YALE MODEL from the 1980s by David Swensen: underweight bonds and harvest illiquidity, basically.

Still, there are some differences.

> The Massachusetts Institute of Technology [says that its massive endowment](https://news.mit.edu/2026/mit-releases-financials-and-endowment-figures-1002), managed by executives who earn more than the university’s president, **earned 10.3% during its fiscal year ended in June**. That’s less than half of what an S\&P 500 index fund earned.

Not that impressive. Weird that the MIT team hadn't done better. Problem? Didn't have SpaceX pre-IPO...

> MIT’s results are more surprising during a tech boom that it might seem uniquely equipped to harness. Harvard and Stanford’s endowments, which held big stakes) i**n SpaceX acquired before its IPO, jumped 27.1% and 31.7%**, respectively. The University of North Carolina, which had more than a tenth of its endowment in that stock, did even better.

Great [Musk](https://stacker.news/items/1600448)-ivite payoff to the "live a little" crowd (https://stacker.news/items/1600985)

> As uplifting as one-year moonshots are, big college endowments offer tuition-free lessons these days about how *not* to invest. Special access to mostly so-so but costly private equity, hedge and venture-capital funds has seen their returns lag what mom and pop investors could have made over the past decade.

## Swansen "could take a very long view, and illiquid investments were cheaper back then."

NOW?

Not so much. Private credit sumbling... everybody wants a piece of the pre-IPO AI hassle. The Robinhoods of the world, whose Venture Fund with early access in some of these AIs, "sports a 3.1% expense ratio, 100 times the cost of an S\&P 500 index fund..." Then again, it's in *their* interest to open *that* bit up to their business... and the Trump Admin have voiced special accounts or bitcoin or private markets in e.g., 401(k)s. **These are weird times.**

> \[Investing veteran Richard] Ennis writes that endowment managers "mostly operate as if nothing has changed" since Swensen's heyday. Allocating 60% to alternatives costs them about 3% annually, or about what Robinhood charges, according to his math.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162883)

***

items.title: Anthropic's Gigantic Net Loss, and Other Cool Stories About Fake Finance
items.text:
This *will* have a Saylor connection (https://stacker.news/items/1600946), *bear* with me...

![](https://m.stacker.news/162864)

So then Mr. Levine goes through three hypothetical scenarios that transfer ownership/economic rights between a company and an outside investor:

1. **Sell 10% of a 10m company on Jan 1.** When Dec 31, company is worth 100m, that outside investor turned 1m into 10m, and the company's original owners have equity worth 90m. The *company* didn't change, but the distribution of owners did (100% of 10m vs 90% of 100m). *This does not hit the company's income statement, obviously*.
2. Company **promises to deliver 10% of stocks to outside investor on Dec 31, against 1m fronted right now.** It's worth 10m on Jan 1 and 100m on Dec 31. It's in some sense a *loan*... but

> For most of the year, the company didn’t have that outside shareholder; instead what it had was, effectively, a bet against its stock. Still, this is basically the same as the first scenario; it’s just a delayed issuance of stock. \[...] **It’s not paying the investor $10 million in cash; it’s just giving the investor the agreed-upon amount of stock.**

3. Company worth 10m on Jan 1, **gets 1m today against a *promise* of cash-settled 10% of company value** at the end of the year:

> Dec. 31, the company is worth $100 million, and it pays the investor 10% of that, $10 million, in cash. The investor has made a $9 million profit. Has the company made a $9 million *loss*? Definitely, right? That’s a real cash payment; the company *just* made a cash-settled bet against its stock, and lost. Pretty clearly this reduces its net income.

> Companies do raise money by promising to issue stock in the future: They sell convertible bonds or warrants, giving the buyer the option to get stock in the future. If a company sells a $1,000 bond that converts into 50 shares of stock when the stock is at $20, and then the stock goes to $50, then the bond is worth $2,500. The bondholder has made $1,500. Has the company lost $1,500? Does it have to reduce its net income by $1,500?

Kind of.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162869)

...and now, for Anthropic's gigantic 80bn net loss for H1:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162873)

.... so, what's up with STRC and MSTR and Saylor? When company goes up in value and fuels itself, perpetual motion machine style, by a) constant inflows via repeated promises to outside investor, and b) when that doesn't work -- which is quite often -- dilute common shareholders by \~1-2% per week... *do you end up with net losses in the company?!*

Of course not accounting wise, but what company management is doing is repeatedly hurling over (new) equity to outside investors for an ever-appreciating company.

**Not sure that's a great idea, browskie.**

***
